en: Preface to the *Continued Abridged Edition of the Five Lamps*:
I have often read the *Five Lamps* and sighed with dismay at the long-standing desolation across successive generations. Is it not the case that there were no great rivers?

Yet when masters arose, those who could fully propagate the teachings remained silent and still. To this day, light is contained and brilliance remains hidden; whose fault is this? Indeed, as for wisdom—

The transmission of these mandates to the world is merely a succession of generations, like the passing of robes. [Question: It is not as if the chroniclers have arisen in clouds; how can the reckonings of good and evil, decline and prosperity within that interval be compared so clearly, as if they were lines inscribed on the eyebrows?

Over time, they will surely become submerged and inevitably tend toward decay. The petty officials compose their "Spring and Autumn" chronicles according to their own whims, and corrupt historians further borrow from them like a marketplace for gold and rice.

The life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is thus hidden... [Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment of a classical Chinese Buddhist discourse concerning historical records and the preservation of the Dharma.]

This has already been entrusted to posterity; what further need is there for written records? Nevertheless, as the generations have become distant and remote, one must judge the three periods of pollution and arrange the five sacred peaks—wherein can one find the true center?
The Longmen inscription recounts three thousand years, encompassing them in fifty thousand words; it is concise yet comprehensive.
Ban Chuan compiled the *Hanshu*, totaling nearly eighty thousand words; it is expansive yet free from excess.
Master Dachuang’s compilation of the *Wudeng Huiyuan* was a merit no less than that of Ban Gu and Sima Qian. Why is it so silent and neglected today?

Our dynasty’s divine sagacity surpasses all others and its subtle principles are widely promulgated; the history of the seventeen years of diligent toil and anxiety cannot be fully recorded, and we grieve [for the neglect of such works].
The rebel has grown insolent and treats our sacred scriptures with contempt; I hear that the halls of the Chancellery are filled to the rafters with nothing but ruins and rubble.
How shall those who come after us rely upon anything? Therefore, I have earnestly discussed this with the Prime Minister Gao Keng, and he likewise shares my concern for these books.

While compiling this history, I earnestly requested that [the authorities] also investigate and collect his surviving writings for inclusion; yet others did not prioritize this, and the matter was ultimately rejected upon internal review.

This is truly a regrettable matter for all eternity. At that time, I was wandering through Mount Wuyi when I happened to receive a letter from the Chan Master Chuan Yuanmen, which mentioned the case of Deng Yuan.
Setting aside my walking shoes, I sighed and said: "The events surely correspond; there must be something lost."
Epistle. The one who selects [the worthy] is Heaven. The Chan Master’s spirit is tranquil and profound; can he encompass all? Can he avoid being indiscriminate?

Is he able to distinguish the turbid from the clear, such that the subtle and the manifest are not entangled even by a single thread? If this is so, he is indeed a pillar of the "Dragon Gate" within the field for selecting Buddhas.
How could he merely halt his steps at the tracks of those great rivers? Indeed, the lineages above and below number some four hundred.
Year after year, his mind followed upon the mind in continuous succession, like a needle threading a bowl; there was not a single flaw or omission. His transcription lies beyond words and letters.
Furthermore, he did not respond to the flowery and redundant praises of the historian Shi [Shenqing] to dazzle and delude future generations.
May the Chan Master exert himself! I am about to withdraw into seclusion, yet I am once again deeply moved by this writing. This serves as the preface.
At this time,
in the late spring of the first year of the Hongguang era (the year of Yiyou), the Buddhist disciple Ma Jiashu, serving as the Left Assistant Censor-in-Chief of the Ministry of Personnel,
respectfully wrote this while bathing his head and body at the Wuyi Hermitage.

An account of the dissemination of the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma) across various records begins with the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* (Jingde Era Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).

Following in its wake were Li Zunxu’s *Guangdeng Lu* (Expanded Record of the Lamp), Foguo’s *Xudeng Lu* (Continued Record of the Lamp), Mengwu’s *Lian deng lu* (Linked Record of the Lamp), and Leian’s *Pudu*... [Record of the Lamp].
The *Lamp* [records] appear in successive layers, its volumes so vast that students cannot help but sigh in dismay at their ocean-like expanse.
During the Shaoding era, Master Dachuang Ji, inheriting the transmission of Zeweng, held the seal of the school and compiled the *Huayuan* (Essentials of the Assemblies) for his fellow students.

This may be called a work where the beginning and end are orderly, unified by a single thread. From the end of the Song dynasty through the Yuan dynasty, there were further masters of the school who spoke [of this].
The Dharma is like the clouds; one could not count its manifestations upon one's fingers.
Entering our Sage Ancestor, the Divine Sovereign, his Way and transformation spread far and wide as the whole world took refuge in him.

Now, meeting this auspicious era, you have emerged with your horns prominent—how could you be compared to Zhu Sheng, who was born too late? Having encountered these final times, I personally witness the bequeathed words of those who were enlightened before me.
Only the Dong and Ji lineages remain, scattered throughout the world; they have not yet been collected and enshrined within the spirit temples.
Master Jipa constantly contemplated this undertaking, yet he never succeeded in accomplishing it.
Even recently, though several far-sighted masters have sought to edit and compile them for many years, none have seen publication. (Zhu) Who would dare to undertake such a task as the narrator?
I have arranged these works in sequence. I fear that as time passes, fame will increasingly sink into oblivion;

as fame sinks, the lineage will become increasingly disordered, with the transmission of teachings becoming unclear and the distinction between the collateral and the principal branches lost. To prevent this, one must take precautions in advance.

Therefore, I have compiled the legacy of the Elder Dachu (Dachuan Lao-ren) into four volumes, printing them to present to the world. Should they encounter a true descendant of Shaoshi who is capable of bearing this burden...
Taking the Buddhas and Patriarchs as one’s own mind, one does not rely on transgression but attains realization through knowledge.

By means of this, one expands and amplifies it, supplementing what has not yet been reached through study and experience, and thereby consolidating a great enterprise. Thus, a thousand lamps will reflect one another, ensuring that the True Dharma flows forth without exhaustion.
I shall wipe my eyes and await this.
Written on the day of the Buddha’s Enlightenment in the seventeenth year of the Chongzhen era, the year of Jia-shen,
by the Dharma-heir śramaṇa Yuanmen Jingzhu of Zhiti Mountain. Bowing in reverence.

The general principles of this work are that the *Huìyuán* (Compendium of Essentials) combines five into one, like pearls strung together or shells arranged in a pattern; the painstaking labor of the skilled artisan is still visible today.

This book has been extensively researched and widely gathered from various sources, discarding the superficial while preserving the authentic. I have not yet dared to offer it for a thousand pieces of gold at Xiányáng, nor...
I intend to present my sincere efforts for deliberation by the world.
This book was compiled over many years; the actual work of recording and drafting began from the winter of the Renwu year of the Chongzhen era through the Jia Shen year.
It has now been completed as a brilliant volume. However, as the four quarters of the realm were beset by many troubles, I concealed it in a stone chamber and did not dare to circulate it.
He continued his travels for another four years until he encountered the passing of his late teacher, Master Shiyu. He then sighed, saying, "The publication of this book has its appointed time.

Thereupon, he appended several of his late teacher's final words to it, following the precedent of the *Zuo Zhuan*, which added the record of Confucius’s death as a supplement to the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
The *Huìyuán* (Collection of Essentials) records that the Caodong school concludes in fourteen fascicles, while the Linji school concludes in twenty fascicles.
That which is completed earlier should be continued first; that which is finalized later should be recorded later. Therefore, the Dongzong (Caodong school) is placed in the first fascicle.
I did not dare to disrupt the sequence of their succession. Furthermore, Yuanzai’s assembly lists Yuanwu as the primary successor, followed by Dahui, and then Huqiu;
this book likewise places the descendants of Dahui first, with the descendants of Huqiu following in second place.

All followed established precedent and there was no deviation from tradition. As for those such as Huanglong Zhong, Yewang Huihuo, Guo Yuan, and others—these few who were transmitters of the lamp—they were appended to the lineage of Dahui’s dharma descendants.
The Linji school first flourished in the Jiangnan region during the late Song dynasty. Through the Yuan and Ming dynasties, eminent masters of this tradition were found throughout the land;
yet they concealed their brilliance and withdrew their auspicious influence, so that the common people could not receive their transmission.

Consequently, only the three lineages of Tiantong, Qingshan, and Chexi stood as pillars supporting China, serving as the ferry and oar for scholars seeking transcendence. However, among these various houses—

The recorded sayings (yulu) exceed what can fill a building; therefore, I have pruned the redundancies and selected the essentials, so that the flavor of a single drop of water may fully embody the great rivers.
As for the various masters of the "Linked Pearls" (lian zhu) and "Eulogies on Ancient Cases" (song gu), their specific monastic residences are not detailed;
I have carefully recorded one such eulogy on an ancient case and appended it to the section on dharma heirs, so that those who examine the lamp records may easily consult them.
The Caodong school flourished especially in Hebei during the late Song dynasty.

This was why Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty assembled such a vast multitude of śramaṇas, with whom only the venerable master Xueting could stand as a towering sage among his peers, clustering like scales.

He was like the *huangzhong* pitch, the foremost of the eighty-four musical modes, or like the hub of a wheel, to which the thirty-six spokes converge. Truly it was a period of supreme prosperity; who could rival it?
I can only regret that from the rise of the Ming dynasty until after the Jin and Liao periods, Hebei became a theater of war.
Famous monasteries were defiled by military camps, and their sacred teachings were ravaged by fire; such was the fate of Baima and Tianqing in Luoyang, and Shaoshi and Longtan on Mount Song.

The empty aspect of Xionger, the Great Illumination of Ci, the Lingyan of Tai, and the Ba’en and Wanshou of Yan—therein the lamps have burned on without ceasing, their lineages clearly recorded. Yet few people have been graced by their light;
until now, only the three branches of Yunmen, Shouchang, and Shaoshi remain, and these are somewhat flourishing. However, from Qingliang upward, there has occasionally been one [lineage].
The two schools’ branches of doctrine can no longer be verified. I ascended Mount Shaoshi to investigate his life’s practices and his final instructions.
In a worn basket, I discovered a manuscript copy of the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings). Its beginning and end were damaged by insects and decayed, making it difficult to infer the full meaning;
however, more than twenty chapters remain legible. By tracing its lineage from master to disciple and comparing it with the *Daoying Taming* (Stele Inscription for Daoxing), all...
The records of the Green Bamboo Society are consistent and harmonious; I have carefully recorded what is most extraordinary to present for the discerning eye.

Regarding the one flower that manifested as an auspicious sign at Mount Bian: the lineage of the Dong lineage branch and the *Kōtō* *Chuanteng* both record that Shilin Xiou was the dharma heir of Lumén Jué, while Wángshān Tǐ was the dharma heir of Yùshān Tǐ. Chúnzhuó Wén...
The "Cai" (才) is a scribal error for "Chun" (淳). Furthermore, there were fewer than twenty-nine generations under Qingyuan;

this was an error on the part of Chan Master Jikong Qibin. This is precisely why Bian Shan, in his tradition of offering incense, identified himself as the forty-second generation of the authentic lineage of Bodhidharma, following the venerable Master Rui.
The detailed analysis of these matters is recorded in the *Dong* [likely referring to the *Dongshan Zhi*].
The Chart of the Authentic Lineages of the Patriarchal Source has not been cited here again.
From the Song dynasty through the Yuan dynasty, there were many eminent figures within the Yunmen school.

For instance, Yuantong Shan and Wangshan Ji were both enlightened patriarchs whose dharma assemblies flourished greatly; however, their lineages of succession cannot be verified. Was it perhaps because they deeply concealed their virtues?

Is it not because they seek to avoid attachment? Or is it perhaps due to the narrowness of their learning and experience in these later traditions? I shall set aside what I do not know, hoping for future attainment.
Recently, my fellow disciples and brothers have arranged the successive entrustments in chronological order; those who first received the Dharma...

The one who arrives first takes the place of honor, while the one who subsequently attains the Dharma follows behind. If there are those nearby who do not follow ancient instruction and wish to regard the one who first opens the hall as the senior, this is not consistent with the principles of righteousness.
To illustrate this through human affairs: suppose there are two brothers of noble standing whose social rank is equal, yet whose entry into official service occurred at different ages.
The younger brother attained glory in the year of the Ox (Chou), while the elder brother entered office in the year of the Dragon (Chen). Yet...

Onlookers would criticize such a person for desiring to rank as an elder brother when he is but a younger; not only would his younger brother feel ashamed of him, but even his father would likely take up a whip to strike him.
Those who read this book will see that it is a transgression of arrogance and the precursor to the violation of hierarchical order.
I am almost certain that you have escaped blame.
The renowned masters throughout the land each transform their respective regions; though one may listen to their reputations and teachings, one does not yet see the whole leopard.

Nevertheless, by ascending the hall and contemplating even a portion of their Dharma discourses, it is sufficient to realize that they possess jade accumulated in Lantian and store gold within the South.
The nation is thus established. Should we encounter a great hand and a vast literary style that further elaborates upon what has been seen and heard, how could we ever repay such kindness?
For this reason, I have composed this "Waiting for the Rhinoceros Horn" (Yangxu).
It belongs to the thirty-fourth generation under the Southern Peak (Nanyue) and the thirty-sixth generation under Qingyuan; these two branches flourish together, upholding the lineage.

His dharma heirs now fill the world. For those who possess recorded sayings (*yulu*) from their time in the world, it is easy to compile them; these have all already been preserved in their initial drafts.
However, regarding their secret practices and subtle applications while dwelling by waterside or beneath forest trees, there is no way to obtain their pivotal dialogues (*jigu*).
If one were to carve them out [into a formal record], would there not be some deficiency? Someone said: "Stop, stop! There will surely be later masters."
Regarding the *Continued Abridgment* (*Xu lüe*): The Secretary-General (Zhao Mengfu) will likely not mind the trouble; why does the Master act so hastily?

Written in the second month of spring, in the year Wuzi, by the Wayman Yuanmen as a casual note on the table of contents for the *Continued Abridgment of the Five Lamps’ Meeting of the Elements* (*Wǔdēng huìyuán xùlüè*).

Do not encroach upon the autumn grasses of Dongling; look instead at the lotus of Shushan in mid-winter.
A monk asked Master Ding of Gaoyou, "What does a golden fish that has passed through the net eat? Ding replied, "Dry dung. Upon hearing this, the Master said, "Thank you for the offering.
The Five Ranks (Wuwei) Verses state: "Centered within Deviation: Deep and profound caves are locked in emerald mist. At midnight, the azure sky is clear."
Like a mirror: A single bright moon ascends the high peaks. Centered within the partiality: At dawn, thick clouds seal the wild scenery;

in the snow-covered hut, spiritual clarity remains as if from a dream not yet awakened, dark and silent as a long, cold night. Coming from the center: A wooden man, carrying his staff, descends the steep heights;
traversing freely, he does not tread upon the ground of the present age; on the stony path, auspicious lotuses bloom beneath his feet. Arriving within the partiality.

Lazily holding the wondrous seal, there is neither true nor false; one sleeps at will amidst the thick green grass. Let the flower-rain fall before the crags as it pleases. Reaching the ultimate within the integration:

the three luminaries have never shone upon this towering peak. Dreaming hands strike the void, and those who hear are rare; standing far apart, it does not fall into the melodies of *gong* and *shang*.
Chan Master Shengmo Guang once composed a verse on Jiufeng’s refusal to acknowledge the Head Seat, saying: "The Head Seat needlessly lost a single stick of incense;
Jiufeng was not disparaging a high worthy. If one were to take 'one color' as the succession, One would betray the former master’s non-reliance on conditions.
Addressing the assembly, he raised the story of Magu shaking his staff and said: "Right is not necessarily right; wrong is not necessarily wrong."
This is neither without a master nor do the myriad virtues not converge. The owl and the cock, day and night, merely exhaust themselves in fragmentation. I lack three inches;
the turtle can only call out to the tortoise. Kāśyapa was unwilling; let him frown as he pleases.
The Second Prince Tu Dan entered the hall and saw Zen Master Chuan of Daming in Cizhou, a successor of Chan Master Renshan Heng, sitting with his face against the wall.
The Prince remarked, "What a fine man of plainness. The Master replied, "Within plainness there is flavor."
Chan Master Wansong Xingxiu of Ba’en Temple in Yanjing was the dharma heir of Chan Master Xueyan Man of the twenty-second generation under Qingyuan. He was a native of Henei and surnamed Cai.
He left the household life at Jingtu Monastery in Xingzhou and took Master Yūn as his teacher.

Later, after receiving full ordination, he traveled with a pack on his back from Tiao to Yan, passed through Tan, and went to Qingshou Monastery to attend upon the elder Shengmo. The master instructed him to contemplate the saying:

"The turning of oneself over to the mountains, rivers, and the great earth," which was spoken by Changsha. For half a year, he made no progress whatsoever. Shengmo said, "I only wish for you to understand it late. One day—

He had a realization. Later, while studying under Xueyan at Daming in Zhi, he examined the saying that "Xuansha had not yet reached the ultimate," and after only twenty-seven days, his intellectual artifice was suddenly exhausted.
Xueyan kept him on as a scribe; their words were in perfect accord, and he was immediately entrusted with the robe and verse.
He then returned to Jingtu Temple, where he built the Wansong Pavilion for his own enjoyment. Thereupon, the venerable elders of the temple earnestly requested him to serve as abbot.
Next, while residing at Wanshou Monastery in the capital, he gave a small discourse (*xiao-can*). Long ago, there was a man riding a donkey who asked a group of monks, "Where are you going?
The monks replied, "To the site of practice (*daochang*. The man said, "Where is not the site of practice? He then struck him with his fist, saying, "This fellow has no sense!
You are riding a donkey right inside the site of practice and will not get down. The man was left speechless. The Master said, "Every person is..."
The Way has a head but no tail in China; one can perform it, yet cannot truly embody it. Little do they realize that this monk’s earlier words do not accord with his later ones.

Since you already know that every lifting and placing of the foot is a site of enlightenment (*dōjō*), why do you not awaken to the fact that riding a donkey or boasting of a horse is nothing other than a Buddha-activity?
Wansong wishes to resolve this unjust case; let me further pass judgment on the flowers.
He said: "A fellow who eats blows and lacks spirit; Maoguang and Du the Chan monk were already unable to overcome themselves—how much more so when they wrongly blame others!
In the place of practice there is but one; the Buddha-dharma is fundamentally not many. I leave this for you, O Kalyāṇamitra, to say: *Oṃ sarva*.

In the fourth year of Mingchang (which is the fourth year of Shaohui of Emperor Guangzong of the Southern Song), the Emperor Jin Zhangzong issued an imperial decree summoning the Master to the inner court.

Ascending the seat, the Emperor personally welcomed him with ritual honors and heard the Dharma he had never heard before; moved by realization and emotion, he personally presented a magnificent *saṃghāṭī* robe made of brocade and silk.

The ladies of the inner palace and the high-ranking nobility prostrated themselves and knelt in reverence, each bestowing their most cherished treasures and establishing a Great Assembly for Universal Deliverance.

The offerings were extraordinary, and for days on end, auspicious clouds stretched continuously across the heavens. From then on, harvests were bountiful and songs of joy filled the roads. This was the Cheng'an era.
In the second year, the Ding-si year, an imperial edict commanded the Master to reside at Xi-yin Chan Temple on Mount Yi in the Capital.

He ascended the hall and said: "The Lotus Palace is specially fashioned as a Brahma-palace; The sacred realm must indeed be visited by the Sacred Sovereign. After the rain, the waters are clear and birds float upon them;
As the rosy clouds brighten, the mountains are still, draped in brocade. Even Tang the Completer unfurled the vast celestial net; Lu Wang rarely cast his moon-soaked hook."
If one asks when such a scene of splendor occurs: it is the autumn of the golden world, when the osmanthus blooms. On the first day of the intercalary fourth month, he ascended the hall and said:
"What is called a man of the Way does not know whether the months are large or small, nor does he know the extra days of an intercalary year.
A wild monk, however, is not like this: this year has three hundred and eighty-four days; last month was a full month, and this month is a deficient month. Thus he spoke.
On the first day of the intercalary fourth month, at the end of the *chen* hour and the beginning of the *si* hour, suddenly someone came forth and said:
"You are indeed thorough, clever, and know how to follow the seasons and measure the times; yet, fundamentally, you lack the breath of the Way. The wild monk covered his nose with his hand and said:
"Keep back! Keep back! What is this 'breath of the Way'? "Take care! He then praised the true nature of Layman Zhanran, saying: "Great!"
Bi Qianbi Juti said, "A single finger was mistaken for a whisk in the hand of Zhanran; it is blind.
Quan Zhen asked, "For over thirty years, my disciple has tried to settle the deluded mind, yet it will not subside. The Master said, "How long has this deluded mind been present?
He asked again, "Originally, was there ever a deluded mind? He asked again, "How would you go about severing the deluded mind? He asked again, "The deluded..."

"Mind-cutting is it; non-cutting is it. Having truly paid his respects, he departed. The Master asked a monk, "Dongshan said, 'The dragon's cry from a withered tree—its strange resonance is difficult to hear.
What is this strange resonance? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "You have a fine understanding of the dragon's cry.
He then asked, "Luminosity and non-luminosity are of one nature and not two. What is this nature that is not two? The Master said, "Heaven."
Xiaobulü asked: "If all Buddhas do not appear in the world, why did they nevertheless take birth in royal palaces? The Master said: "The green mountains constantly lift their feet.
He asked: "And yet there is no nirvana; why did they nevertheless pass away at the twin śāla trees? The Master said: [The green mountains constantly lift their feet.]
"The white sun does not shift its wheel. [The student] asked: "Why does one who has let go on that side not abide in the central position?

The Master said: "Great achievement is without a master. [The student] asked: "Why does one who turns back to this side not fall into a peripheral region? The Master said: "Ultimate transformation is non-action.
[The student] asked: "You told me before, 'Do not go; returning, you will turn your back on your father. How can one avoid turning their back on their father?"
"Go," the Master said. "Be careful not to look back. A monk asked, "It is difficult to let go of mind after mind. What is the person who has let go? The Master said, "Carry it away.
A monk asked, "Every place is Maitreya; there is no gate and no Sudhana. Why then do you say, 'In the crystal palace, there is no teacher'?
The Master said, "Once the palace is demolished, we shall meet. In the evening, he resided at Baoen Temple and subsequently retired from his post.

At Cong’an, he addressed the assembly: “Where the wheel of the karmic mechanism turns, even the eye of wisdom remains deluded; when the precious mirror is opened, not a speck of dust can pass through.
When the fist is opened, it does not fall to the ground; responding to things, one must know the proper time. When two blades meet, how can one avoid a collision?”
Addressing the assembly: If you go, I will detain you; if you stay, I will send you away. Neither going nor staying—He has no territory. Where can one meet Him?
Everywhere, in every place—tell me, what kind of thing is this that is so extraordinary? Addressing the assembly: To move is to bury oneself ten thousand fathoms deep;
not to move is for sprouts to grow right where one stands. You must let go of both ends and look into the middle.
"Put it down! Only then can you buy straw sandals and travel on foot. Addressing the assembly: "Kicking over the vast ocean, the great earth flies into dust;

shouting away the white clouds, empty space shatters to pieces. Even the strict disciples and established commands are but half-extracted. When the Great Function is fully manifest, how can one provide for it?
Addressing the assembly: "The single pivot beyond is a crane soaring into the Milky Way; the direct path before us is a hawk passing overhead."
Xinluo (Silla). His eyes were as straight as a *niao* gong and resembled shooting stars; yet he could not avoid having a mouth like a flat carrying pole. Tell me, what was his fundamental teaching?

The Master was thoroughly versed in the studies of Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the hundred schools of thought. He examined the Tripitaka three times and constantly practiced the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
One hundred and twenty people attained the Dharma from him. He lived to the age of eighty-one.
Chan Master Xueting Fuyu of Shaoshi in the Western Capital was a dharma heir of Chan Master Ba’en Xiu of the twenty-third generation under Qingyuan.
He was the son of the Zhang family of Wenshui in Taiyuan. While his mother was pregnant with him...

His mother repeatedly experienced extraordinary dreams. At the time of his birth, auspicious omens appeared one after another within the household. By the age of five, he could speak and comprehend a thousand words daily;
at nine, he entered school and could read ten lines at a glance. The local community bestowed upon him the title of "the Holy Child.

Not long thereafter, he encountered the disturbances of the former Jin dynasty during the Zhengyou era; having lost his siblings, he was left solitary and without support. On the road, he met an old man.
A bhikṣu invited his teacher to leave home and study Buddhism, saying, "If you can recite one fascicle of the *Lotus Sūtra*, your affairs for this lifetime will be concluded.
The teacher said, "Does the Buddha-dharma end here? Is there perhaps no further message beyond this? The bhikṣu was struck by his insight.
They then went together to visit the ancient Buddha Xiulín at Xiānyán, saying, "This youth is a dragon-elephant (a great being)."
[He was] a seed [of great potential]. "If I may serve as his attendant to provide him with towels and combs, he will surely become a vessel of great capacity in the future.
The Ancient Buddha (Wansong) joyfully accepted this, and thus shaved his head and conferred upon him full ordination. He subsequently served alongside Master Guang of Shuangxi for seven years.
At that time, Wansong was residing at Ba'en Temple in Yanjing; without seeking an introduction, the Master simply strode off alone to visit him. Upon seeing him, Wansong...
He granted his seal of approval. From that time on, he remained in close attendance for another ten years. Thereafter, the Way flourished even more and his fame became increasingly renowned;
those who studied under him grew ever more numerous. During the upheaval of the Renchen year, his ancestral monastery fell into ruin.

Soon after, he succeeded Wansong, and Haeun again invited him with a formal letter, whereupon he received the command to go to Shaolin. While Sejo was still in the imperial residence, he commanded the Master to compose a [text].

He participated in the Assembly for the Support of the Precepts. On the day of Wushen, an imperial edict appointed him to reside at Xingguo Monastery in Helin. Before a month had passed, he was summoned by Emperor Xuanzong to the imperial tent.

His responses to the Emperor’s inquiries were to the Emperor’s satisfaction, and he was commissioned to preside over the Buddhist teachings. He restored two hundred and thirty-six monasteries that had been abolished, thereby reinstating the monks and nuns.

On the day of Gengshen, when Emperor Shizu ascended the throne, [Liu] discussed and identified apocryphal scriptures; he dispatched an express courier to report this, and the books were subsequently burned.

He was further bestowed with the title "Guangzong Zhengbian" (Orthodox Discernment of the Radiant Ancestor). An edict was issued to establish a vihāra named Ba'en (Gratitude) in his native village, providing fields and goods for the sustenance of the monastic community.
At that time, there was no one capable of succeeding to the patriarchal seat at Wanshou Monastery; the assembly requested that the Master preside over it.
Subsequently, he established branch temples in Helin, Yanbei, Chang'an, Taiyuan, and Luoyang. In the eighth year of the Zhizhi era (1271),...

In the spring of the Xinwei year, an imperial edict was issued for the monastics throughout the empire to assemble in the capital. Those who were his dharma-heirs accounted for one-third of the assembly—how magnificent!

The Master possessed a brilliant and awakened nature; after reading the Tripitaka three times, he had mastered it by heart. He guided and assisted later students without ever showing signs of weariness.
He was well-versed in a multitude of secular works and excelled at calligraphy and verse composition. His formal sermons and general discourses amounted to nearly one hundred thousand words.

It was circulated among the monastic community. Someone wished to carve it for publication in the world. When the Master heard of this, he rebuked him, saying, "This was merely something I uttered in a moment of playful sport;
how can it be treated as a formal record? Later, weary of receiving visitors, he retired to Sōngyang.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master replied, "Wait until the Milk Peak nods its head."
"I have told you. [The student] asked, "What is the one path of supreme nobility that transcends all? The Master said, "A fisherman’s song startles the herons from the sandy islets;
they fly out through the reeds, and their tracks are lost. The Master then asked a monk, "The source of the Way is not far away; the ocean of nature is not remote."

"Tell me, where is it? The monk failed to respond with realization, and the Master gave a shout. On the twentieth day of the seventh month in the autumn of the Yihai year, he manifested slight illness.
He wrote a verse to announce his passing. His secular age was seventy-three; his years since ordination were fifty-two. He was interred in a stupa at the western corner of the monastery.
Chan Master Conglun of Yanjing Baoen Linquan first took up residence at Wanshou Temple.

He ascended the hall and said: "Zen, Zen—neither orthodox nor biased; it has no path of intention, yet possesses a profound abyss. It transcends the present and surpasses antiquity, cutting off what follows and illuminating what precedes.

If one can simply forget traces and shadows, why need one cling to the raft? To point directly to the human mind and see one's nature, one must rely on the patriarchal intent to penetrate the mystery. [Nine years...]

The true message of facing the wall: there is indeed a secret transmission within it. In the ninth year of the Zhizhi era of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty, he was summoned to the inner palace for an audience.
The Emperor and the Imperial Preceptor (Imperial Master) commanded the Master to expound upon Chan. He then cited Guifeng’s *Chan-yuan chuan-shi*: "In Sanskrit, this is called dhyāna;
here it is translated as 'cultivation through contemplation,' and is also termed 'meditative concentration' (samādhi). These are both general terms for meditative absorption and wisdom."

It is so named. Chan is the source of all virtues; therefore, it is called the *dharmatā* (Dharma-nature). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that it is also the source of sentient beings’ delusion and awakening;
therefore, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-store). The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that it is also the source of the myriad virtues of all Buddhas;
therefore, it is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature). Thus it is said in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. However, Chan has both shallow and deep levels, with distinct stages and grades.

That which is practiced while harboring heterodox views, longing for higher realms and loathing those below, is the meditation of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika-dhyāna*). That which is practiced with correct faith in cause and effect, likewise through longing and loathing, is the meditation of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-dhyāna*).
That which is practiced after awakening to the principle of the partial truth of self-emptiness (*ātma-śūnyatā*) is the meditation of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna-dhyāna*).
That which is practiced after awakening to the ultimate truth revealed by the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is the meditation of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-dhyāna*).

"If one awakens to the fact that one's own mind is originally pure, fundamentally free from afflictions, and that the nature of impartial wisdom is inherently complete, then practicing in accordance with this is the Meditation of the Supreme Vehicle; it is also called the Pure Meditation of the Tathāgata.

That which has been transmitted through successive generations since the time of Bodhidharma is precisely this Pure Meditation of the Tathāgata. The Emperor said, "In the past, whenever questions were asked..."
[The Emperor] said, "You speak of 'no speech. Why then do you now have this speech? The Master replied, "In principle, there is fundamentally no speech;

for now, I shall speak by way of phenomena. The Emperor asked, "For what reason is principle beyond words? The Master replied, "Principle is realized through spiritual communion. It is like a person eating honey:
if one asks about the color and appearance of the honey, one might describe it as purple or white; but if one discusses the description of its taste, it is truly difficult to express."
The Emperor asked the Imperial Preceptor, "Is this statement correct or not? The Preceptor replied, "This is no different from the profound Prajñāpāramitā found within the scriptures.
He then asked about a *gong'an* (public case) of the Patriarchs. The Preceptor cited the incident concerning the Sixth Patriarch and the wind and the banner:

"It is not the wind moving, nor the banner moving; it is the mind of the noble one that moves. The Imperial Preceptor said, "In reality, it is the wind and the banner that move; why do you call it the mind moving?"

The Master said, "All things are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Is this not the movement of the mind? He debated this point until evening, then emerged from his quarters and dispersed.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The Northern Dipper resembles a ladle; the Southern Dipper resembles a gourd. Let them measure as they please.

Warm sun and cool breezes—the winter solstice and the Cold Food Festival on the one hundred and fifth day—one must know that the seasonal rhythms do not yield to one another. Reaching this point, is there anyone who understands?"
"Swallowing and spitting out—how? A monk asked, "Fayan said, 'For twenty years I understood this only as an objective realm.

Since it is not to be understood as an objective realm, how should one understand it? The Master said, "The monkey carries its young back behind the green peaks; the birds sing and flowers fall before the azure cliffs.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "If we discuss this matter, it is like a phoenix soaring through the sky, leaving no trace of its passage. It is because of this.
The nature of reality is empty and vast; the sun of wisdom is brilliant and clear. It illuminates that the five aggregates are all empty, causing the myriad conditions to vanish together.

One directly attains a state where stars cluster in the azure void and the moon encroaches upon the vermilion steps; emerald curtains hang down, incense burns, and all is silent. At such a moment, how could one permit even a breath?
How could one allow for peeping or intruding? The secret chamber does not admit a breeze; the profound gate offers no foothold for the foot.
"Even so, a single point of luminous spirit pervades the universe; how could it be confined to India or Caoxi?
On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the eighteenth year of Zhizheng, by imperial decree, the false scriptures of the Daoist canon were to be burned at Minzhong Temple in Dadu.
With the exception of the *Daode jing*, all were to be completely incinerated. The Master was ordered to set the fire, whereupon he struck with a torch."
The first circle says: O virtuous ones! As for the sacred texts of the Three Caverns (*Sāndòng*), are they able to testify to this Fire-Light Samādhi (*Huǒguāng Sānmèi*)?
If you can realize it here, then you already possess the *Beidǒu Jīng* (Scripture of the Northern Dipper) at home; to teach others otherwise would be to cause their mouths no peace.
If this is not yet so, then after the ashes have flown and the smoke has vanished from this point on, even if you search everywhere for the Celestial Honored One (*Tiānzūn*), how could you find him?
Look with a fixed gaze.
When Chan Master Congkuan was nearing death, he asked his second elder brother, "The Buddhas, the Patriarchs, and my parents—I have now shot them all dead with a single arrow.
What do you think of this, Second Brother? He then adjusted his robes and passed away while sitting upright.
Chan Master Quan-yi of Huayan Monastery in Shangdu was the son of the Hao family of Xingzhou. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent, surpassing other boys.

At the age of six, he shaved his head and went to attend upon Wansong. Possessing a vast memory and extensive learning, his discourse and debate were unhindered. Wansong appointed him as his attendant;
whenever he heard one of Wansong’s verses or dharma discourses, he immediately understood them thoroughly, and thus he received the Dharma. He served constantly as an attendant.

In responding to others on his behalf, his spiritual acuity was unassailable. Liu Chengzhong, the Grand Protector, recommended that the Master was highly capable for great service. Emperor Shizu summoned him for an audience and, after conversing with him, was greatly pleased.

He remained at the royal court, offering much counsel and benefit. After three years, he was sent back home, whereupon the Emperor conferred upon him the title "Great Chan Master Puguang of the Buddha-land.
In the fifth month of the Dingsu year of the Zhizong era, he manifested illness and passed away reclining on his right side.
A rare fragrance persisted for three days. He was cremated, and his *śarīra* relics were innumerable.
The Chancellor Yelü Zhinqing, a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) whose courtesy name was Chuci, was originally surnamed Yelü.

When the Jin dynasty extinguished the Liao, he returned to the Jin and changed his surname to Yelü. Initially, when the Master was in the capital, there were many masters of Chan; however, among them, only Chenghe of Sheng'an...

Master Shang alone held him in high esteem and frequently consulted him regarding the Way of the Patriarchs. He repeatedly questioned him about what he had gained from the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of the venerable masters of antiquity;
occasionally, Sheng’an would grant his approval, leading the Master to believe he had attained realization.

However, upon encountering personal misfortune and distress, he placed his ambition for fame and achievement on a high shelf and sought the Way of the Patriarchs with even greater urgency. Consequently, he once again came to consult him regarding these former matters.
"Master Sheng'an, your interpretation of the case is not what I perceive. I am greatly perplexed by this.
Sheng'an replied with composure, "In the past, when you occupied a position of high authority, many Confucian scholars did not earnestly believe in Buddhist scriptures;

they merely plucked out phrases and anecdotes to serve as topics for conversation. For that reason, I did not dare to apply rigorous scrutiny. Now, I judge that your heart is truly [seeking the truth]."
You have asked me about the fundamental matter. How could I continue to repeat my former errors and fail to speak with bitter urgency? I am old;

there is one known as Old Man Wansong, who is fully equipped in both Confucianism and Buddhism, is thoroughly proficient in both the Chan school and the scriptural teachings, and possesses unimpeded eloquence.
You may go and see him. Once you have studied under Wansong, you must cut off all human traces and cast aside domestic affairs, even in the face of severe cold or humid heat.

There was not a day that he did not engage in study. Burning oil lamps to continue his work by the light of day, he neglected sleep and forgot to eat for nearly three years before finally attaining verification [of his realization].

He was given the title *Jianran Jushi* (The Layman Jianran). His preface and critique of the ancients runs briefly as follows: "The Buddhas, patriarchs, and various masters have their roots buried ten feet deep;

the hundred cases of karmic conditions sprout shoots upon seeing the world. Tiantong [Yunwen] ought not to have pulled up the branches, and Wansong [Xingxiu] could not bear to extend the vines. Jianran..."
However, this merely adds thorny ropes to the existing branches. It pierces the nostrils of those who merely seek fragrance and chase after scents;

it trips up the heels of those who practice the profound and embody the subtle. If you wish to have your heels touch the ground and your nostrils reach toward heaven, you must first pass through these very tangles.
Previously, when the former sovereign was about to set out on his western campaign, the officials...
The memorial stated: "Among the monastics at Mount Wutai and other locations, there are those skilled in incantations and military tactics, as well as those endowed with great physical strength;

these should be made into troops for our western expedition. The Duke stopped him, saying: "Those who are high-ranking practitioners of the Śākya school must strictly observe the precept against killing."

They revere the practice of compassion and patience; thus, there are those who would rather risk their lives than take a pearl from a goose, and those who would rather die than pluck a blade of living grass.
They reverently carry out the laws and decrees of the Dharma King, not transgressing them even unto death. How could it be appropriate to employ such as these in military service?

Those who do not follow the laws and regulations certainly lack noble resolve and conduct. Since they have already violated the Buddha’s intent in that [monastic] realm, how could they possibly be loyal subjects here in this kingdom?
For these reasons, none of them could follow the Imperial Army. The Emperor followed this advice.
In the sixteenth year of Taizong’s reign, the Master passed away at the age of fifty-five (which was the third year of the Chunyu era of the Southern Song).
The twenty-fourth generation descendant of Qingyuan, Chan Master Wen Tai of Lingyin at Shaoshi in the Western Capital, was a dharma heir of [Shaoshi] Chan Master [Xinghua].
His clan and lineage are unknown. The Master possessed an extraordinary intelligence that surpassed others and was profoundly devoted to the Dharma.
Delighting in the School of the Lineage (Zongcheng), he subsequently traveled to Shaoshi Mountain. Before long, he realized the essential point of the mind;

thus, among those of his time who were called the "high disciples of Xueting"—namely Er Tai and Yi Su—he was one of them. He ascended the hall and said: "The events of kalpas past are present right now;
the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all within the source of the mind. Try to have him present this face-to-face, and then there will be no more [doubt]."
"Understand this by picking it up against the wind. Now tell me, where does the fault lie? He struck the ground with his staff and said:
"Precisely because it is so exceedingly clear, it causes what is attained to be delayed."
Chan Master Zhitaï of Zhonglin at Baoen Temple in Taoyuan Prefecture was the son of the Wen family of Yucheng in Fenyang.
Having shaved his head and studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he sighed deeply and said, "A man of great character should investigate the Great Matter; how can one confine oneself to such trivialities?
At that time, Xueting presided over Wanshou Temple, and the Master went to rely upon him for several years. His realization became transcendent and peerless. [The Emperor's] Court...
He called upon his teacher’s name and proclaimed that he would dwell in gratitude. One day, manifesting illness, he gathered the assembly and said, "My life’s span ends here.
You must each protect and uphold yourselves well; cherish every moment and do not let it pass in vain. Those who heard this were all moved to tears. He then wrote a verse, saying:
"By practicing the teachings of Master Zhong, I have built a seamless stupa; By casting down my own self, I have realized the formless body. No..."
He manifested a body with marks and a body without marks; within this body without marks, he remained aloof from even a speck of dust.
Having finished writing, he passed away peacefully. Chan Master Jing Su of Zu’an at Lingyan in Taian Prefecture was a native of Yongping in Baoding.
His clan name was Zhang. He took Shousheng of Xiangshan as his teacher and studied under him for over twenty years, meeting ten enlightened masters along the way.
The others [of his lineage] finally attended Xueting at Wanshou. Having spent many years refining himself in practice, he was bestowed with a robe and a verse of transmission.

Initially he presided over Wanshou; next, at Shaoshi and Lingyan; later, he retired from the seat at Xiangshan. One day, he assembled the congregation to take his leave and passed away in the right-side reclining posture.
Master Zhonglin composed an inscription for him, which says: "The nostrils that pierce the heavens; the heels that touch the earth; the mind is luminous."

His gaze was upright; his conduct was ancient and his countenance was warm. As his deeds grew ever greater, his resolve became ever more earnest. Elder masters from all quarters repeatedly knocked upon his door. He received the lineage of Xueting and became a grandson of Wansong.

His wheel of spiritual machinery turned with the speed of a flash of lightning or a roll of thunder. His lofty banner towered above the tree of enlightenment, and he firmly consolidated the sacred roots.
The lamp of wisdom shone brightly, dissolving the masses of darkness. With his total capacity and great function, he shook and stirred all things.
Heaven and Earth: He overturns the Bohai Sea and kicks down Mount Kunlun; he swallows all Buddhas of the three periods in a single gulp.
Not lingering in the two extremes, what need is there to discuss the Middle Way? Dwell in the great monasteries as the fourth assembly reveres him.
Coming and going leave no trace; movement and stillness are without mark. Though empty space may crumble away, this Way remains forever.
Chan Master Huan-yuan Fuyu of Bao-ying Temple in the Western Capital, a native of the Wang family of Ling-shih in Huo Prefecture,
was a dharma successor of Chan Master Shao-shi Tai of the twenty-fifth generation under Qingyuan. He relied upon [the monastery] of his home district...
He received the tonsure at Tuṣita Monastery and traveled extensively among lecture halls, where his eloquent discourse flowed like a stream.

Later, hearing that Master Lingyin possessed a perfectly clear eye of the Way, he devoted himself to him for investigation and study. One day, hearing Master Yin ascend the hall and cite the words, "One must not seek from others;

to do so is to distance oneself from me," the Master attained sudden enlightenment and immediately received formal certification. He first presided over Tianqing Monastery, and subsequently at Baoying. A monk asked:
"What is the great meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master replied: "The wind carries the sound of the spring to my pillow;
the moon shifts the shadows of the flowers to my window. He passed away in the tenth month of the Gui-chou year of Huangqing at the age of sixty-nine, with forty-nine years since his ordination.
Chan Master Qiu Jiangjie of Lingyan in Jinan Prefecture was visited by Xuexuan. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? Xuexuan replied, "From Qingzhou.
The Master said, "Did you bring the Qingzhou cloth robe with you? Xuexuan said, "I have already presented it to the Master. The Master silently gave his approval.
He then had Xuexuan attend the meditation hall for a long time. One day, his long-standing doubts were suddenly dissolved like melting ice. Directly—

He constructed a "Cubit-Sized Room" (zhàngshì). The Master said, "The mysterious gate secured by golden locks has been opened. Xuán said, "Within a peach pit from a thousand years past, what old kernel do you seek?
The Master nodded in approval and instructed him, saying, "This is that which you inherently possess; guard and maintain it well."
"One day, it will surely be you who can propagate my Way.

Chan Master Yungak Yongda of Westing Baoying Temple was a dharma successor of Chan Master Insan Sook of Inryang. He was a native of the Liu clan of Fenzhou and received the tonsure in his home prefecture.
At Tianning Temple, he constantly used the transcendence of birth and death as his motivation for seeking instruction through southern travels.

Hearing that the Dharma-thunder of Lingyan resounded afar, he traveled there on foot from a great distance, drawn by the reputation of its virtue. Upon first meeting him, Lingyan recognized his potential; after long and intimate study, he finally entered the profound depths of the teaching.
He then said, "Realization is attained through the teacher, but its practice lies with oneself. Thereupon, he went to Taian Prefecture to close himself in retreat. His Way—
The laity pressed him earnestly with invitations; having no choice, he arose. One day, manifesting illness, he passed away peacefully.
Seon Master Poju of Bongnongsan was born into the Liu clan of Huya. At fifteen, he went to Chonggyeong to leave the household life and studied under Iryeon.
Iryeon subjected him to the hammering of the fundamental essence, refining him further until his attachments were suddenly shattered like bursting sparks.

In the sixth year of the Dade era, Chan Master Yue’an Hai retired from his position at his home temple. He prepared a formal petition for the opening of a new hall and was bestowed the title of Great Chan Master Miaoyan Hongfa.
Shortly thereafter, he was granted the posthumous name Longjian; the Master was requested to accept these honors, but instead returned to seclusion at Lingqi.
He passed away at the age of seventy-seven.
Chan Master Xiangyan Chunzhu Wencai of Dengzhou,

a descendant of Qingyuan in the twenty-sixth generation and a dharma heir of Chan Master Baoying Yu, was born into the Yao family of Linfen in Pingyang. From birth, he possessed extraordinary qualities.

Zhi was a man of remarkable character; whenever he saw a monk, he would join his palms and prostrate in greeting, unlike ordinary children. He took up the monastic life under Master Fuyan Pu at Mingfuyan Monastery in Jiangzhou.
Once, while reading the *Song of Realizing the Way*, he reached the line, "The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body," and attained a joyful realization.
He then went to visit Chan Master Huan Yuan to present his understanding, and the Master approved of him. He subsequently spent three years studying the Tripitaka at Longmen Mountain.
In the year Jiazi of the Taiding era, he presided over Shaoshi Mountain. He subsequently retired to Xiangyan, where he expounded upon the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* and the *Huayan fajie guan*.
A monk asked, "What is the Dharma-realm of Principle? The Master said, "When empty space falls to the ground, it shatters into pieces that form no pattern.
The monk asked, "What is the Dharma-realm of Phenomena? The Master said, "When you arrive, the house is utterly cleared away; thus one avoids becoming [a mere phenomenon]."
Wuyongwu asked, "What is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena? The Master said, "In the three months of winter, withered trees flourish;
in the nine months of summer, snowflakes fly. He asked, "What is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between all phenomena?

The Master said, "The clear breeze accompanies the bright moon; the rustic old man laughs as they draw near. On the seventeenth day of the fifth month of the Renchen year of the Zhizheng era, he bathed and changed his robes.
He summoned his disciples and issued this admonition, saying, "When I die, do not perform elaborate rites; it would be a mere waste of fire. It is sufficient to scatter my ashes.
At dawn the following day, he passed away in auspicious signs. His entire body was interred in the Snow Court Stūpa (Settei-tō) to its right. He was eighty years of age.
Chan Master Xuexuan Daocheng of Tianjie Monastery in Jinling was a dharma heir of Chan Master Lingyan Jie. He was a distant descendant of Prince Zhao of Yunzhou;
his father moved to Baoding, where they subsequently made their home. At the age of fifteen, he left the household life at Xingguo Monastery in his prefecture. The Master had a broad forehead.

Ping’e was a man of imposing and majestic bearing and possessed great ambition. After receiving full ordination, he formed a group of three as companions and dwelt in an earthen cave in Qingzhou, where they secretly investigated the core meaning of the single transmission.
Suddenly, an old man of remarkably ancient appearance appeared and said to them, "You three have forgotten both hardship and ease, and have delighted in simplicity and detachment;
you have investigated and clarified the Great Matter of the Ultimate. In days to come, you shall surely become the Dharma-gate."
"The pillars and beams have departed. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Since you are a pillar and beam, why do you dwell within an earthen cave?
The old man replied, "There has never been one who constantly travels without dwelling, nor one who constantly dwells without traveling. Having spoken, he vanished.
The Master redoubled his diligent efforts in secrecy. Later, hearing that Master Jie of Qiujiang was greatly propagating the teachings of the Caodong school at Lingyan in Qi, he went there.

After paying his respects (as detailed in the "Inscription for the Pure Chapter at Insan Hermitage"), he returned to Cheongsaha. The assembly requested that he reside at Pujosa. Initially, he stayed at Daejaksan Mountain in Dongnae.

In the fifteenth year of the Hongwu era, provincial and county governments were established throughout the realm with *sengsi* offices to oversee the Buddhist teachings; the Master was selected for this appointment.

His spiritual affinity with the Prince was such that the Prince’s enlightened favor toward him was exceptionally profound. In the eighth month of the autumn of the thirtieth year, the Master was summoned by imperial decree.
Upon arriving at the hall, the Emperor commanded him to reside in the celestial realm. The Master submitted a memorial stating that he did not understand the Buddha-dharma.

The Emperor composed a poem, engraved upon a golden plaque and suspended in the Dharma Hall, which read: "Not answering the words of greeting, I permitted his silence; Returning west with his single shoe, the ancient single transmission.
In the empty King’s Hall, drums and bells ring on the first and fifteenth; The seat is shown as it was many years ago. He ascended the hall. [The clouds] were ten thousand white...
In a brief moment of unfolding and rolling up, the true mechanism beyond kalpas is revealed; the thousand peaks of crimson leaves blaze forth, manifesting the wondrous principle within.
Unfailing throughout antiquity and the present, it remains ever-present through the passage of dust-like kalpas. The bird-path is empty yet penetrating; one takes steps at the profound pivot.

The lion’s string is dense and continuous; the fingers press down with rhythmic precision. Ancient tones ring out in resonance, until even the stone woman nods her head and the wooden man claps his hands.

With his hand, he picks up a golden nail and a jade thread, threading them through the vanguard of the mechanism. He cuts off the horns of a hare and the hair of a tortoise to reveal that which transcends the ordinary.
The orthodox and the deviant are revealed alone, and the hidden and the manifest are fully encompassed.

After the Emperor personally led the hundred officials in performing the rites of sacrifice and offering, he visited the Master’s chamber. From the void, he inquired after his well-being and bestowed several *ding* of precious paper currency.
He ascended the hall and said: "The Yin reaches its limit and the Yang returns; the days of transformation grow long. Plums everywhere emit their fragrant scent."
The message within this is not much; how could it ever be concealed throughout the entire realm? Thus, clearly manifesting and encompassing the hundred grasses, it meets us at our very heads.
It proclaims secretly and intimately, revealing itself alone amidst the radiance of the myriad phenomena. On the field of profit and fame, recognize the True Person of No Rank;
amidst the mountains of self and other, display your original face. Its shadow contains the mirror of the school.
When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; the body is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). When the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
A barren woman holds aloft the precious seal, its patterns fully manifest; a wooden man silently passes through the golden shuttle, not missing even a hair’s breadth.

He pulls the mechanism of the wheel beyond kalpas; his blazing radiance pervades the years and months within the world. Reaching secretly both the distant and the near, he causes flowers to bloom upon withered wood.

Comprehending both the ancient and the modern, it causes flames to burst forth from within the freezing ice; clouds shroud the ancient path, where the lingering wild colors once again lead one astray.
When the moon fills the cold crags, its brilliant divine light shines everywhere; when the mechanisms of the six gates have ceased, there is no need for circuitous detours or indirect references.
When the single color is perfected, one must strictly avoid being "sealed through" at the head. When the white ox sets its steps, it already receives the conditions for transformation;

when the jade horse neighs in the wind, it is entirely a matter of benefiting sentient beings. But tell me, what is the matter that transcends this? *Pah!* A staff of rabbit horns picks up the moon from the bottom of the pond;
a whisk of tortoise hair hangs the clouds atop the ridge. [Ascending the hall: "The three yang energies intersect in harmony, ten thousand..."

All things are renewed. This reveals the wondrous function of the One True Reality and encompasses the profound source of all transformation. In every atom the Way is united; everywhere there is a passage through the ford.
The Dharma assembly is grandly inaugurated and the Garden of Enlightenment is widely opened. The destiny of the nation rises together with the destiny of the Buddha;
the imperial breeze fans forth alongside the wind of the Patriarchs. Just as it is said that the old year has passed and the new year has arrived, I wonder: from where does the passing depart?
"Where have you gone? Where have you come from? Such deliberations only serve to increase confusion. I dare ask the assembly:

within the single stroke beneath the patched robe, is there still any addition of coming and going? If you can realize this, you will see that as the year ends, the harmony of the sun brings forth the shadowless tree;
as spring returns, flowers bloom on branches that never sprouted. [Ascending the hall: In the fifth month, the hibiscus flowers shine upon the eyes.

Clear. With fragrant breezes and singing birds pervading the mountain retreats, there is no mystery or subtlety in that one move prior to the mechanism; one must simply avoid recognizing form and sound for oneself.
Recall how Chan Master Heshan Shouduan addressed the assembly, saying: "There is no dharma before the eyes; the intent lies right before the eyes."
"It is not a dharma of the present moment; it is not something reached by the ears or eyes. Tiantong Jue said:
"Old man Jiashan has untied his sack and scattered rare treasures before everyone. At such a time as this, what then?
'The roads have no lost articles'—this is what the gentleman praises. But tell me, O assembly: [what of] Jiashan and Tian[tao]?"
If one examines the views of the two masters, Tong and Er, one by one, they are all found to be full of leaks and flaws. Fengshan’s approach is not like this:
if one perceives forms or seeks sounds, that is not the family treasure. To truly know that not a single dharma exists before one’s eyes—this is it.
Every single thing and every single object is in total accord. Should this not yet be so, listen further to the final phrase: "When the Way is prosperous, the Son of Heaven does not issue commands;
when times are peaceful, one need not sing songs of great tranquility. In the seventh month of the thirty-fifth year, Emperor Taizong Wenhuang ascended the precious throne.
The Master was dispatched as an envoy to the Kingdom of Japan to proclaim the Sage’s transformation. In the second year [of his reign]...
The officials on the mission submitted a memorial, and the Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased; his favor and patronage were even more abundant than before.

In the fourth year, while over a hundred of his subordinates and associates were imprisoned for nearly a hundred days, the Master remained composed and free from anxiety. The Emperor, knowing they were innocent, pardoned them.

In the spring of the sixth year, he received an imperial decree to establish a Great *Pudu* (Universal Deliverance) *Zhāi* (Fasting Rite) at Mount Zhongshan and commanded the Master to preach the Dharma.

The audience numbered tens of thousands. In the eleventh year, he traveled to Beijing for the New Year’s court celebrations. By imperial decree, he was commissioned to hold a vegetarian feast at Qingshou Monastery;
his gifts and honors were especially abundant. In the third year of Xuande, when the Master was seventy-six years old, he submitted a memorial requesting to return to the mountains.
Emperor Xuanzong Zhang, moved by his sincerity, dispatched palace attendants to escort him back south to the Western Hermitage of Tianjie Monastery to dwell in seclusion.
Lao. On the eighth day of the twelfth month of his seventh year, he manifested a slight illness. He took leave of the assembly, spoke a verse, and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
The Emperor dispatched an official to present a written memorial of sacrifice. He was eighty-one years of age and seventy-five years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*).

On the day of his cremation, the smoke and flames were five-colored; immortal cranes soared through the sky, and a wondrous fragrance drifted through the air. Over ten thousand people, including officials, nobles, and the fourfold assembly, witnessed the event.
All marveled at its rarity. After the fire, they collected countless round, red-colored śarīras and erected a stūpa outside the Ande Gate of Yingten County.
By imperial decree, the site of the stūpa was granted the name Juefeng Chan Temple.
Chan Master Xianan Yirang of Tianqing Temple in the Western Capital was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fenglong Jue. He was the son of the Li family of Zhending.

Having shaved his head at the age of seven, he traveled extensively to consult with the masters of the school. Finally, he went to Mount Fenglong to seek out the chamber of Guyan; upon seeing him, Guyan praised him highly.
He was honored with this title. In the second year of Zhizhi, he opened a dharma hall at Tianqing.
Subsequently, he moved to Kongxiang on Mount Xiong’er, Lingyan on Mount Tai, and Songshao in Luoyang. In the summer of the Gengchen year, he fell ill and addressed his disciples, saying:
"This illness cannot be cured; I shall surely depart. You must urgently prepare a stupa. On the twelfth day of the fifth month, the construction of the stupa was largely completed.
The Master entrusted his final affairs and then wrote a verse, saying: "When coming, it was originally still; when departing, it is likewise perfect and pervasive.
The void performs a dance, wandering freely as it pleases. He then passed away lying on his right side.
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Shaoshi Cai of the twenty-seventh generation under Qingyuan:
Chan Master Songting Ziyen of Wannan Temple in Nanyang Prefecture, from Fan Village in the ancient Guoushi County of Henan.

As for his surname and origins: he suffered from many illnesses in his youth. His parents, out of pity for him, permitted him to follow the teachings of Śākya. He paid homage to Yún at Shaolin, and at the age of eighteen, he received full ordination.

The Master was exceptionally intelligent and surpassed others; he was widely versed in both Buddhist and secular classics. Regarding poetry and prose, he possessed such innate ability that he could compose them without study.
Whether responding to verses or composing on the spot, his pen moved with effortless fluency. Great masters and eminent scholars all regarded him as a vessel of the Dharma.
First he studied under Jiang Yuezhao, then under Xianan Rang, from whom he received instructions on the essentials of Chan and experienced a moment of awakening.

Later, he studied under Chan Master Chunzhuo. Zhuzhe subjected him to repeated examination and discernment using the *Precious Mirror Samādhi*, which completely cleared away his doubts and obstructions.

Zhuzhe said, "The responsibility for carrying the Great Dharma rests entirely upon your shoulders," and subsequently transmitted to him the robe and the Dharma. [He was like] a lion atop the Five Milk Peaks.

"Son of a son! His words transcend the masses, illuminating those who came before and those who follow. At that time, the seat at Wannan in Nanyang Prefecture was vacant, and he was invited to preside over it.
Upon entering the second year of the Hongwu era of the Great Ming (the Jisi year), he took charge of Shaolin, where he personally labored in the fields to provide for the community.
The Verse says: After the chaos, I returned home to till the soil myself; Who can discuss the hardships of this rustic life? By day, I pick up clods of earth to drive away mountain birds;
At night, I sit in my thatched hut to chase off wild pigs. My heart breaks as the autumn wind frequently strikes the watch-tower gong;
I gaze at the night moon, my soul consumed by sorrow. Only recently have I come to know the bitterness of the farmer; With every meal, I still think of the kindness of the donor. (13)
In the winter of that year, His Majesty King Zhou respectfully commissioned the Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma for the sake of the posthumous merit of the Empress Dowager Chizaokyo.
The King bestowed upon him a *saṃghāṭī* robe as a mark of distinction. Later, having reached the age of seventy, he...

Chan Master Ziding of Songxi on Mount Xiong’er in Shan Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Tianqing Rang, was the son of the Ma family of Yan’er. At the age of seven, he paid his respects to the Ancient...
Yan shaved his head [to become a monk]. Upon Yan’s passing, he went to attend upon Xian’an, who was then serving as the Librarian (Zangzhuchi).

Under the Master’s guidance, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment. The Master’s interrogations and discernments were as formidable as the frost of autumn or the scorching sun; yet his spontaneous responses to circumstances were like a pearl rolling across a platter.
One day, manifesting illness, he said to his disciples: "My worldly karmic ties have come to an end. I shall pass away in accordance with the natural order."
"The time has come. You disciples must not harbor worldly attachments. Listen as I deliver the final word.
Having spoken thus, he lay upon his pillow and passed away in stillness.
Chan Master Nengran Liaogui of Shaoshi on Mount Song,
a dharma successor of Chan Master Wanan Yan of the twenty-eighth generation under Qingyuan, was born into a flourishing clan in Jindian, south of Mount Song.

From the age of seven, he fixed his mind on the school of Emptiness and knew there was a matter concerning his own person. He subsequently took refuge at Shaolin, where he first donned monastic robes at the age of twenty.
Initially, he visited Yueyin at Xiangshan; though he passed through many seasons of cold and heat, he was rarely able to achieve realization.
Chan Master Songting presided over Tianqing Temple. The Master went there to rely upon him and consulted him daily regarding his own spiritual practice, yet he could not finally put his mind at rest.

One day, as Song was ascending the hall for a discourse, he said: "A single word, utterly transcendent, uniquely extricates one from the present moment. At that, the Master was immediately relieved and attained clarity.

He retired to the hermitage of the Second Patriarch. In the twenty-third year of the Hongwu era, the seat at the ancestral temple was vacant; the entire mountain community made earnest requests for him to return, but the Master declined with all his might.
Unable to refuse, he arose in response to the conditions and ascended the hall. He said: "Do not seek the standard within words; you must clarify the essence beyond the phrase.
If you can understand it in this way, you will penetrate past and present, free and at ease. Do you know? This continued until the Yongle era."
In the nineteenth year of his reign, while in good health, he suddenly summoned his assembly to bid them farewell. He spoke this verse: "Eighty-seven years of life;

From evening until evening again. Casting off my hands beyond the limit of voice, It is continuous and dense. Throughout his life, the Master’s conduct had been upright and dignified, earning the deep reverence of kings and princes.
When the three royal princes—Yi, Sa, and E—of Zhou and Shu ascended the mountain to make offerings, they presented him with generous gifts.
Zhenbei. His manner was as pure and untroubled as flowing water.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Shaoshi Gaizhi, the twenty-ninth generation descendant of Qingyuan.
Chan Master Qi Bin of Shaoshi on Mount Song was a native of Yuanqu in Pingyang. He studied under Ningran, seeking instruction on the essentials of the mind.
He consulted his teacher morning and evening, and one day, upon seeing a Qin-era cypress tree, he attained sudden enlightenment. He immediately returned to attend upon his master.
Upon seeing him once, [Master] Yitian said to him, "Qibin has attained Chan; the profound essence of the Dongshan school resides within you.
In the fourth year of the Jingtai era, he presided over Shaoshi. A monk asked, "What is the matter prior to the empty kalpa? The Master replied:
Turtle Facing Fire.
A descendant of the thirtieth generation under Qingyuan,
the Dharma heir of Chan Master Shaoshi Bin.
Chan Master Wufang Cong of Dingguo Temple in the Western Capital was the son of the Xu family of Luoyang. He received the tonsure at Fuxian Bi峰 Temple.
Initially, he visited Longtan Shunchao and Chaozhua Zong; upon entering their chambers to seek instruction, he attained a degree of realization.
Later, he went to Shaoshi to study under Chan Master Jukong, who subjected him to further refinement through his dense and profound methods of training. Once, while examining...
Dengyuan saw that the five practitioners had all summoned the Venerable Baoshang due to certain causes and conditions;

the Master immediately attained a secret realization of the profound meaning of the Five Ranks and subsequently received his seal of certification. He then remained in seclusion at Dingguo Temple in Guairu, where he addressed the assembly:
"The ancestral vehicle of the Buddhas is fundamentally beyond words and speech; however, this style of our house is not obtained from without. One must undergo the 'sevenfold interrogation.'"
The mind. Only when you can discern the seeing through the eight returns will you arrive home securely, no longer traversing the path.

Regarding these various methods mentioned above, you must be most careful and cherish them. He passed away in the sixth month of the nineteenth year of the Chenghua era; his age was sixty.
14. Forty years in summer. Enshrined at the ancestral tomb on Mount Shaoshi.
