"Monk? the Old Man asked. The Master immediately struck him with his staff. The Master caught it and said, "Do not say that there is no monk here.
The Old Man nodded his approval and immediately invited him into the position of Attendant. When the Old Man passed away, the Master went to Jingci Temple to rely upon Chan Master Shilin Gong.

Shilin appointed him as a Secretary (Jishi). He subsequently visited Xueyan, who asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From the Two Zhe regions. Xueyan asked, "For what reason do you speak..."
The sounds were not the same. The Master said, "Close that foul mouth! Yankuan said, "The Taji Bridge is high; the Jiyun Peak is steep. I do not yet know where the record-keeper is.
The Master clapped his hands and said, "The duck swallows the snail; its eyes bulge out. Yankuan laughed and looked back at his attendant, saying, "Serve some fine tea.
The Master said, "That is unnecessary. This was the fourth year of the Dade era, the *gengzi* year (1060), when he departed.
He was a source of merit for the world, and his disciples flocked to him until his fame reached the capital. By special imperial decree, he was granted the title Chan Master Huíwén Zhèngbiàn.
Subsequently, he presided over Zhōngtiānzhú. In the *rénzǐ* year of Huángqīng (1312), he moved to Línyìn.

An imperial edict was issued to establish a Great Water-Land Assembly at Jīnshān, and the Master was commanded to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. He was further granted the honorary title Fórì Pǔzhào. In the *rénxū* year of Zhìzhì (1322)...

He succeeded to the abbacy of Mount Jing Mountain. On this occasion, he was thrice bestowed with the gift of a golden-embroidered robe. On the day he opened the hall for formal discourse, a monk asked, "What is it like before reaching Fengshan?
The Master said, "A single path where pines and cypress trees grow old. The monk asked, "And what is it like after arriving? The Master said, "The majestic presence of a thousand peaks.
A monk asked, "What is the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye? The Master said, "The Stone Gannang at the crossroads."
[The Master] said, "Is it not just this that is so? The Master said, "The moon is like a drawn bow; there is little rain and much wind. A monk came for an interview.
The Master asked, "From what direction do you come, O Sage? From where do you come, O Spirit? The monk replied, "I am right here before Your Majesty.
The Master said, "Careless Chan practitioners are as numerous as hemp and millet. Go to the meditation hall! He then examined another monk, saying, "The chessboard stone shall split open your skull."

"The bowl-basin pool has soaked and rotted your soles. The monk prepared to answer, but the Master gave a shout. (Nanshi Xi said: "What business is there in this? [It means: What reason is there for such an approach? He then examined another monk, saying:
"The splendor of Mount Hua piercing the heavens is split asunder; the Yellow River is released, its depths utterly clear. Let that be for now."
"Bring forth a phrase from the ground of reality. As the monk prepared to open his mouth, the Master struck him. He ascended the hall and said: "The autumn wind is cool; the autumn night is long.
The traveler who has not yet returned thinks of his hometown. He struck the meditation seat and said: "From this point on, one will not return; once one returns, it is attained.
Over the misty waters of the Five Lakes, who would dare to contend? He ascended the hall again and cited the Great Master Bodhidharma, who said: "I originally sought the mind..."
Do not seek the Buddha. To thoroughly understand that the three realms are empty and devoid of substance is not as good as sitting upright and quietly observing the mind.
This very mind, mind after mind, is the Buddha. The Master said: "This would be to 'sit and kill' Master Bodhidharma. Entering the hall for discourse, he said:

"Set aside the Buddhas of the three periods of time; put the six generations of patriarchs on the other wall. For now, during the twelve hours of the day, you must simply recognize [your own nature]."
The master of one’s own house takes charge wherever he is; in every place where he stands, there is truth.

Unshaken by the five desires and the eight winds, and unable to be confined by the four modes of birth or the nine realms of existence—only then does one have a slight degree of resonance with reality. Let me ask you this:
while wearing clothes, eating food, defecating, urinating, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—which of these is it?
"You, my master! There are some people who recklessly speculate within the eighth consciousness, claiming:
'When called upon, there is a voice, yet its form is not seen; right now, as we speak and respond, this vivid, solitary clarity—is this not my own master?
They are mistaken. This is the very root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas."
Since the beginning of kalpas, the deluded mass of karmic consciousness has caused you to stumble and fall in every direction, subjecting you to myriad sufferings and a thousand hardships.
How can you possibly recognize this as real? Apart from this, after all, who is your own true master?
Again, he called out in a loud voice: "Master! Wake up! He then ascended the hall. At the ancient watchtower, the morning drum sounds.
The Horn. An empty mountain at night answers the bell; People of the time all listen together. Where would it not be perfectly pervasive? Ascending the hall, a monk asked:
"When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why did the monastery steward’s eyebrows and beard fall off? The Master said: "When one house has trouble, a hundred houses are busy.
The monk turned his head and called out, "Everyone, take note! The Master said: "Today this old monk does not wear [his robes]."
He then said: "If one discusses this matter, it cannot be sought with a mind of intentional effort, nor can it be attained with a mind of non-attainment.
It cannot be constructed through words and language, nor can it be communicated through silent stillness. Within the twelve periods of the day, how then can one achieve resonance?
Here, the wind is somewhat harsh; wait until we return to a warm place to deliberate. [This concludes the] lecture on the Lantern Festival. And...
Director of the Abbot’s Quarters, Bath Master, and Rector: A thousand grains and ten thousand grains are born from a single grain. From where does this single grain arise?
A thousand lamps and ten thousand lamps originate from a single lamp. From where does this single lamp arise?

If you understand one lamp, then for a thousand lamps and ten thousand lamps, there will be no doubt regarding each and every light. If you understand one grain, then for a thousand grains and ten thousand grains...

Grain by grain, there is no obstruction. A three-legged donkey trots along, prancing its hooves. It tramples through the boundless seas of fragrant water. Holding up his staff and striking it once, he said:

"Even at the crown of one's head, not even a single grain may be lacking. On the fourth day of the eighth month of the Xinsi year of the Zhizheng era, he wrote this verse to bid farewell to the assembly:
"Fundamentally there is neither birth nor extinction; how could there be going or coming? The river of water blazes with flames."
The iron tree blossomed; he cast down his writing brush, extended one leg, and passed away. His entire body was enshrined and interred in the Jizhao Pagoda Courtyard.
Chan Master Yishan Liaowan of Jiangxin Temple in Wenzhou, a successor of Chan Master Ying of Jingci Temple, was the son of the Jin family from Linchuan in Fuzhou. He was fifteen years old when...

Master Chengwen was renowned for his literary talent; however, his long-standing aspiration was to leave the household life. Unable to dissuade him, he went to Jinxi Changle Monastery to receive the tonsure.

When Dongsou took charge of Nanping, he selected Master Ze to serve as the *jishi* (recorder). One day, while passing by a shrine, the Master saw paper ashes swirling upward with the wind; he suddenly forgot everything he had realized.
He immediately reported this to Dongsou, who questioned him about it until the Master was finally free from all doubt and hesitation. Thereupon—
Having received his seal of approval, he later traveled to Tiantai. The assembly invited him to open the Dharma at Hanyan; subsequently, he moved to Zituo, Shushan, and Kaixian.

He ascended to reside at Jiangxin, yet whenever he felt slightly dissatisfied, he would immediately abandon his post and depart. It happened that Master Chan Master Yuejian Ming of Mount Lu sent a boat to welcome him back to Dongxi.
When Master Ming passed away into nirvana, the assembly of Kaixian again requested him to return. The winter of the first year of Huangqing—
He fell ill and, having written his parting instructions, passed away while seated.
Chan Master Yitang Yi of Yue-lin, Mingzhou, was a native of Wenzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said, 'I have no dharma here to give to people;
I simply settle the case based on doubt. The Sage of Zhangsheng also said, 'I likewise have no dharma here to give to people.'"
He did not rely on doubt to reach a conclusion. Holding up his staff, he asked: "What is the Buddha? Treading barefoot upon lotus flowers.
"What is the matter beyond the Buddha? Carved beams and painted rafters. He then cast down the staff and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
On the fifteenth day of the second month, he ascended the hall and struck his whisk once, saying: "Today, Zhangsheng shall stir the cold ashes of thirty years ago."

"From within, he bursts forth black beans to exchange for Old Hu’s eyes! He lets out a shout and says, "If there were a dharma that surpassed nirvana, this one shout would not function as a single shout."

Chan Master Huiji Yuanxi of Yangshan in Hongzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yuwang Guan. He was the son of the Tang family of Nanchang. Both he and his elder brother, Yuanling, pursued the studies of the jinshi examination.
Once Yuanling had passed the examinations, the Master subsequently shaved his head. He heard that Wuchu was expounding the Dharma at Yujiji.

He went to rely upon him. At their first conversation, [the Master] was greatly amazed by him and kept him in his service. Morning and evening he questioned and consulted him until all the secrets were revealed.
In the second year of the Yuanzhen era, he emerged into the world at Baiyang, and later moved to Jingci. Ascending the hall, he said:

"Yunmen uttered the word 'Universal' (Pu), such that no one in the entire world could do anything about it. Yet they fail to realize that Yunmen’s four corners were firmly planted on the ground. At that time, had he..."
He gave a shout with a thundering roar, waiting for this old fellow to show his wickedness. Then, slowly performing a formal greeting (*wenshun*), he said, "Do not take offense at my intrusion.
This was not merely to rescue this old man; it was also to revitalize the fundamental principles of the Yunmen school. Nevertheless, the mouth is the door to calamity.
On the occasion of the opening of the retreat, he ascended the hall and, making the gesture of tying a cloth bag with his hand, said: "Today, Nanshan ties this cloth bag."
"The mouth of the bag is open! You all, each and every one, should dwell in the sameness-wisdom (*samatājñāna*) within your own body and mind.
Should there suddenly be someone who breaks through the azure sky and knocks down Mount Sumeru, do not say that the knot was not firm and dense;
you must know that there are hundreds of thousands of layers of the celestial net. After spending three months at Qianjingshan, the Master took up his staff and returned to Nanshan.
After this, he rose again; he did not depart. When the scholars of Jiangxi heard that the Master had retired from his post, they all turned their hearts toward the flavor of the Dharma.
Consequently, the disciples of Baizhang and Dayang vied with one another to invite him. The Master, unable to decline, eventually returned to Mount Yang.
After residing there for three years, as he was about to pass into *nirvāṇa*, he composed a verse for the assembly, threw down his brush, and passed away at Mount Dayang.
Below is the Jinji Stone (Golden Cock Rock), where he was interred in accordance with the prophetic prediction of Master Ma.
Chan Master Jingci Wen was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yunfeng Miaogao of Jingshan in Hangzhou; he was a native of Funing Prefecture. He studied under Xianxi, and one day, Xianxi—
For example, it is like an ox passing through a window lattice: its head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through, yet why is the tail unable to pass?
The Master had a sudden realization and replied, "The whale swallows the sea water entirely, revealing the coral branches.
Xike approved of this. Later, he entered the world and resided at Daliu. In the Gengchen year of the Zhizheng era (1340), he moved to Jingshan. Ascending the hall, he said: "Before the world..."
Form: Heaven and Earth are in profound stillness; before the birth of Buddhas, they were not yet fully manifest. To behold the body as it is, one is entirely true.

Without cause, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) leaped forth from the eagle’s nest and tore off his own face-skin. Having already been subjected to the brushstrokes of those who depict him, why does he further show missing teeth?
This old barbarian did not abide by his own proper measure; seeing that the Eastern Land of China possessed the capacity for the Mahāyāna, he traveled ten thousand miles from afar with this intent.
Amidst the scramble for profit and the seizing of markets, it has come to the point where the drums resound in the Phoenix Hall and the bells toll in the Arhat Pavilion.
Every turn of the throat strikes a taboo; every step taken finds no door. The entire nation is unable to pursue him, and he is once again exposed.

The new Abbot of Jiangshan, driven by necessity, has boarded another’s boat and entered another’s domain. A new official does not attend to old affairs—after all, what is to be done? Striking the meditation seat, he said:
A pavilion completed, silently storing the moonlight of a thousand peaks; wild grasses spread out at leisure across ten thousand miles of autumn. Entering the hall:
Five peaks stand steeply—only those who are such people may reach them. A single mirror hangs in the sky; there is nothing that does not receive its illumination.
The ancestral patriarchs’ foundation remains as it was; the livelihood of the patch-robed monks has never undergone change. Where one cannot lay a hand, this is precisely where one must be uplifted.
Tear it apart! Only when there is no door through which to set foot may one truly tread upon the path. Wait until the mountain clouds grow faint and the stream water flows murmuring;

until there is a single melody of selflessness and ten thousand prostrations of joyful practice. At such a time, where does the merit reside? Since ancient times, the chariots and books have been one;
the script and tracks have been as uniform throughout the four seas. Now that we share a single family, there are those who praise or revile the Chan school. The Master sighed and said: "This..."

"I shall endure this dispute for the sake of the Great Vehicle of our school," he said, and proceeded to the capital. An imperial decree was issued to assemble the followers of the various schools for a court debate.
The Emperor asked, "What is the fundamental principle of Chan? The Master replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and still.
It cannot be reached by seeing, hearing, sensing, knowing, thinking, or discriminating. Although the Emperor questioned him repeatedly, the Master cited examples from the Western Heavens.

From the patriarchs of the Eastern Land down to the instances of the staff and shout of Dezhanshan and Linji, it is generally held that Chan is the treasury of the true Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, and the path to the Supreme Vehicle.
His discourse on the attachment to existence being greater than [attachment to] Chan was explicit in its phrasing and amounted to over two thousand words.
Furthermore, he invited Yang Qian and the Master of the *Śataśāstra* (Bǎifǎ Lùnshī) to share seats with him at Xianlin, instructing each of them to uphold [the teachings].
Lin said, "From the Deer Park to the end at the Bahudā River, not a single word was ever spoken during this interval.
From where did these five thousand-plus scrolls come? The Master said, "The temporal teachings of a lifetime are like a finger pointing at the moon;
one must understand that what the finger points to is ultimately not the moon. Lin asked, "What is Chan? The Master struck him with his hand.
Yuanxiang drew a circle. Lin said, "How can you move your hands and feet? The Master said, "Even this single circle cannot be penetrated;

what need is there to speak of thousands of sutras and ten thousand treatises? Lin was speechless. The Emperor was greatly pleased. Upon taking his leave to return south, he addressed the assembly, saying:

"I originally intended to remain deeply hidden in mountain caves, secluding myself until my time had passed. I did not expect that with the All-Illuminating Heaven looking down upon me, it would be difficult to escape its ultimate transformation. Furthermore—

He said: "With the patched robe on the head, all affairs are at rest; at this time, even the mountain monk does not understand. He passed away, and his stupa was erected at the western foot of the mountain.
Chan Master Zhihong Jian of Tiantong in Mingzhou composed a verse on the story of Dayang’s "Formless Dharma Hall," which begins: "True Emptiness..."
Formless and beyond names or models; the foundation established is subtle, while the painting produced is coarse. To speak of it is not difficult—these words are set upon paper.
The bearded man from the Western Heaven has no beard at all.

Chan Master Zuyun Yuetai of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Peng of Shuanglin. He was the son of Zhou [family] from Nankang. One day, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he reached the passage:
"The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all atoms. Suddenly, he had an awakening. He went to see Bieshan, who asked him:
"From where have you recently departed? The Master replied, "Jiangxi. Shanshan asked, "Is the Great Master Ma doing well?
The Master joined his palms and said, "I pay my respects to the Abbot. Shanran went to see Duqiao and asked, "Is it true that Linji was struck three times with a heavy staff by Huangbo?
The Master said, "Yes. Shanran asked, "Why did he then punch Daoyu in the ribs three times? The Master said, "When one receives a bull from another, one must return a bull to that person."
Miaoxi (Ma) nodded in agreement. After Miaoxi passed away, Jishi (Jie Shi) filled his position. One day, while in the meditation hall, Jishi raised the "Pine Tree" koan.
As the Master was about to offer a response, Jishi shouted, "Why do you not say: 'Before the Yellow Crane Tower, the Parrot Isle'? At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
After some time, he returned to Mount Lu and took up residence at Xilin. In the ninth year of the Dade era, he resided at Lingyin.
Once, he interrogated a monk, saying, "The myriad Buddhas of the fine dust are upon your tongue; the holy teachings of the Tripitaka are beneath your feet.
Why do you not suddenly awaken? The monk was at a loss. The Master then gave a shout. He again interrogated another monk, saying, "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his slaves.
Who is he? The monk prepared to respond. The Master then struck him. A newly arrived monk entered. The Master asked, "Where have you come from?"
"Where have you come from? he asked. "From Minzhong," [the monk] replied. The Master said, "How is the Dharma maintained there?
"When hungry, one eats; when tired, one sleeps," he replied. The Master said, "Wrong. "I do not know how you maintain the Dharma here, Reverend," he asked.

The Master shook his sleeves and returned to his quarters. After staying for four years, he bid farewell to the assembly with this verse: "Coming through the convergence of conditions, departing when conditions disperse. *Zhuang*..."
He overturned Mount Sumeru; empty space was revealed alone, and he subsequently passed away.
Chan Master Yingong Jie, the Dharma heir of Chan Master Xuedou Yaoweng Bingtong of Qingyuan Prefecture, was the son of the Zhang family of Xinchang. He first followed Chijue...

At Tiāntóng, he next went to the abode of Dàchuān. When Dàchuān raised the story of the "Mountain Burning on the Full Moon of the Twelfth Month," the Master was about to respond when Dàchuān suddenly struck him with his bamboo staff;
at that moment, he attained realization. He remained in seclusion, carrying his staff and closing his door to transcribe the *Lotus Sūtra*.

There was a verse that read: "Old age does not mean one must shun guests; in stillness, I wish to copy the sūtra. At that time, the seat at Xuědòu was vacant, and the assembly earnestly requested [him to take it].
The Master then proceeded. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the year Renyin, he ascended the seat and exhorted the assembly with words of extreme compassion and urgency;
this was because he was indicating his departure. When the assembly requested that he leave behind a verse, he smiled but did not respond. At evening, he passed away.
Chan Master Chengjian Yusou of Zhiti Mountain in Funing Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Wuwen Can of Jianfu Temple. He was the son of the Zhang family from Ningde in that same prefecture.
He received the tonsure at Longshan in Zhenghe and subsequently attended Chan Master Wuwen Can, eventually entering his inner quarters. He first resided at Baiyun.
In the twentieth year of the Zhizhi era, Emperor Shizu issued an imperial edict bestowing upon him the abbacy of Zhiti and the honorary title of Grand Master Tongwu Mingyin.
Later, when he manifested his passing, he wrote a verse: "For eighty-two years, I have been deceived by worldly conditions; now, with a somersault, I shall manifest my traces in the Western Heaven.
Having bathed and changed his robes, he sat in the lotus position and passed away.

Chan Master Xijiang Mou of Tiantong, in Qingyuan Prefecture, successor to Chan Master Huazang Jing, addressed the assembly: "A spring day is bright; the oriole sings—how most intimate! Who can understand it?
One day, as he was about to enter extinction, he looked at his attendant monk and said: "A smile, turning over the body: the face of the sun, the face of the moon."
Facing [the wall], he set down his brush and passed away.
Chan Master Kong of Zhongtianzhi in Hangzhou, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Jue of Mount Jing, gave this instructional phrase (chuyu) within his quarters: "Casting gold to form iron."
The Real Man of the Eastern Sea offered this eulogy: "The young master in brocade robes, intoxicated at a rustic farmstead, Slept soundly upon a wooden bed while the sun had not yet risen.
Calling for hot broth and gruel, he received nothing; He thus traded his jade belt for a bowl of tea."

Chan Master Chou-an Zong, of the lineage of Chan Master Huanglong Keshi, ascended the hall at Huguo Monastery in Hangzhou and said: He cited Chan Master Yuelin Zhen’s instruction to the assembly, which asked:
"The mouth of the cloth bag is open; is there anyone who would buy? A monk said: "There is. Yuelin said: "Neither as something expensive, nor as something cheap."
"How will you buy it? The monk was speechless. Lin said, "The old monk has lost out.

The Master said, "Yuelin’s statement of the question was quite extraordinary, yet as soon as someone spoke the word 'there is,' he was left with nothing but to cover the east and hide the west, unable to conceal it fast enough.
Today, Huguo opens the mouth of his sack; is there anyone who can buy it? After a long silence, he said, "The railing."
Though the poles lean together, the mountain views appear differently.
Chan Master Wenzhou Xialu Wujian composed a verse on Xinghua’s beating of Kebin, which says: "Xinghua beat Kebin."
To speak with intimacy yet lack true intimacy—like raindrops from the tip of a staff, they strike forth the Jade Qilin.
The layman Yu Fangniu was a native of Old Hangzhou. During the Chunyou era, he studied under Wumen.
Whenever he asked a question, Wumen would block him head-on, saying, "Not so, not so. Later, upon meeting Chou'an, he asked, "What is your teacher's realization? How dare I..."
Regarding the inversion of right and wrong among humans and devas, Wumen said, "Under my seat, there is no dharma to be attained and no path to be transmitted;
I have obtained only two words. The scholar asked, "How can you speak of these two words? Wumen replied, "Not so, not so.
At these words, the scholar finally understood how Wumen dealt with people. He composed the "Passing Through the Barrier of Right and Wrong," in which he stated: "Direct pointing..."

The human mind: seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood. Turn the light back upon itself; it is utterly free from obstruction. The moment you attempt to deliberate, ten thousand miles of white clouds intervene.

Meeting people, you judge them with praise or blame; encountering things, you rate them as superior or inferior. You hold the ancients in high esteem while disparaging the present, valuing what you hear over what you see.
Let them speculate as they will; even in their lingering reflections, they have not yet dreamed of the barrier between right and wrong. How can you penetrate it? For now, look at this: what is it?
The primary meaning: when answering, one must not break one's teeth; instead, one displays spiritual powers to cross the river in secret.

There is a share of toil that does not approach the noble. Seeking with the mind, I grant you peace. Great pain, silent and piercing to the very bone—plucking leaves and seeking branches is not the work of a master hand.
The Western Heaven remains as dark and vast as ever. Where there is a Buddha, one must not dwell. The swallow carries [the spring] away.
Carrying away the spring colors; when the cuckoo cries, snow fills the heavens. Ten thousand points of fallen red petals are the rain of longing. Where there is no Buddha, pass quickly by;

one is unwilling to sit within the precious palace of the Awakened King. Having practiced for six years before coming out of the mountains, only then did he believe that the axe-head is indeed made of iron.
When the laywoman Shen Daopo of Anji Prefecture asked, "How many phrases are there regarding the barrier of right and wrong? the Master said:
“There are four propositions. Ba said, “How would you raise these four propositions? The Master said: “The first proposition, that there is both right and wrong, is not acceptable.
The second proposition, that there is neither right nor wrong, is also not acceptable. The third proposition, that it is both right and wrong, is not acceptable.
The fourth proposition, that it is neither right nor wrong, is also not acceptable. Only when one can transcend these four propositions does one finally see.”

[The questioner] said, "What is the scenery of one's own native ground? The Master said, "Can you leave it? [The questioner] said, "I cannot leave it. The Master said, "Everyone has their lot; why can you not leave it?
[The questioner] said, "When a chicken is married, it flies after the chicken; when a dog is married, it runs after the dog. The Master asked, "What is the scenery of one's own native ground?
The Master said, "The moon is full and round, shining upon how many continents? How many people rejoice, and how many..."
Chou said, "I do not ask about this 'wind and light' (fēngguāng). The Master said, "Then you ask about that 'local wind and light' (bědì fēngguāng)?
Chou said, "That which has no marks of male or female. The Master said, "Since there are no marks of male or female, what 'gate of right and wrong' (shìfēi guān) could there be to ask about?
Chou said, "Is there anything further beyond this? The Master said, "There is. Chou asked, "What is this thing further beyond? The Master said, "A locust clings to a heron."
Yijiao. "When you ascend to heaven, I shall ascend to heaven.
Chan Master Gufeng Xi was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhengning Wanshan of Gushan in Fuzhou. He was a native of Taishu in Shuzhou and surnamed Li. [He resided at] Monsan.
"Param! The Master asked, "The radiant, silent illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges—is this not the words of the scholar Zhang Zhuo?
As Shanshan was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him with his staff and shouted him out. The following year, Shanshan attained enlightenment.

He returned to the abbot’s quarters, and the Master asked, "The radiant, silent illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges—is this not the words of the scholar Zhang Zhuo? Shanshan then overturned the meditation seat. The Master—
He then seized him and said, "Where is the point where your words fell? Yunmen covered the Master’s mouth with his hand. The Master asked, "Where is the error?
Yunmen said, "A second offense will not be tolerated. The Master said, "Recite another verse. Yunmen immediately recited: "Yunmen acts strangely;
he cannot help but defeat himself. A lion bites a man; a hunting dog chases a clod of earth. The Master said, "The staff..."
"On another day, I will give you a meal. Baoshan said, "If the Master requires it, I shall lend it to you. The Master picked up his bamboo staff and struck him three times;
Baoshan then bowed and departed. The Master remained in Min for over thirty years, and the fourfold assembly revered and admired him.
To the end of his life, he wore plain cloth and used paper quilts, remaining untainted by anything of the world.
Chan Master Jie of Shuanglin in Wuzhou composed a verse on the circumstances of the Great Master Fu putting on his patched robe and donning his crown, saying:
Neither Confucian, nor Daoist, nor yet Chan, His improvised practice is truly pitiable.
Leaving this one body unfinished in three ways, To this day, more than eight hundred years have passed.

One night, Chan Master Zhonghe Zhang of Qingshou Monastery in Yanjing, a successor of Chan Master Yong’an Hai, dreamed of a strange monk who, leaning on a staff, walked directly toward the abbot’s quarters and sat upon the lion throne.
At dawn, he told the guest prefect: "Today, whenever there is a traveler seeking lodging, have them come to see me."
When it grew late, Haiyun arrived. The Master smiled and said, "This patch-robed monk is the one I dreamed of last night.
Yun said, "I have come without coming; how shall we meet? The Master said, "In study, you must study truly; in awakening, you must awaken truly. Do not merely dig up old stumps.
Yun said, "Because sparks flew when I struck the fire, I realized that my eyebrows are horizontal and my nose is straight."
The Master said, "In my place, it is different. Yun asked, "How do you express this conviction? The Master said, "The teeth are a set of bones; the ears are two pieces of skin.
Yun said, "I thought there was something else. The Master said, "Wrong. Yun gave a shout and said, "The grass-thief is utterly defeated!"
The Master retired. On the following day, the Master raised the case of Linji’s two head monks of the two halls both shouting at once when a monk asked, "Is there still guest and host?
Linji said, "Guest and host are clearly distinct. How do you understand this? Yunmen said, "Shatter the mirror of the Qin dynasty; sharpen the ancient awl.
When the dragon soars beyond the azure heavens, what need is there to strike it further with a mallet? The Master said, "You..."
He had grasped the pivot, but not its function. Yun then overturned the meditation seat. The Master said, "The pleasures of the road do not yet mean one has reached home.
Yun gave him a slap and said, "A thousand-year-old wild fox spirit; now that you have been seen through, you are not worth a penny.
The Master struck with his whisk and said, "You have grasped its function, but not its essence. Yun stepped forward.
The Master said, "The green mountains tower with a cold hue; the moon shines upon a single stream amidst the clouds. Yun said, "You have attained its essence, but you have not attained its wisdom.

The Master said, "Though you are skilled in the samādhi of eloquent speech, it still has no connection to the matter. Yun raised his fist and then snapped it once. At that moment, the Master... (Note:
The source text ends abruptly with "丈," which typically refers to the Master's staff or a measure of length, suggesting the narrative was cut short.)
The room shook. The Master said, "So it is, so it is. Yun brushed his sleeves and departed. The next day, the Master appointed him as the Record-keeper (Pal-zhi).

He further tested him with the "upper-tier" hammer and tongs of the Dharma; Yun’s responses were entirely in accord. One day, the Master said to him, "You have now reached the ground of great peace and bliss.
You should maintain this well. I possess the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Nirvāṇa of the Patriarchs."
"I entrust this mind to you in secret; do not let it be lost. Yun covered his ears and departed. The Master then bestowed upon him a verse, saying:
"Heaven and earth share the same root; there is no difference or distinction. Where, among the mountains of one's home, would he not be encountered? I now entrust to you the Seal of the Empty King."
The Radiance of the Myriad Dharmas is Universally One.
*Wudeng Huiyuan Xulüe*, Fascicle Two, Part One;
*Wudeng Huiyuan Xulüe*, Fascicle Two, Part Two.
Compiled by the Chan monk Jingzhu, a successor to the Patriarchs at Mount Zhiti,
a twenty-generation descendant of Nanyue and dharma heir of Chan Master Duan of Mount Jing.
Chan Master Xingyuan Huiming of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Xia family of Huangyan in Taizhou.

Having grown up, he was dissatisfied with remaining a layman and went to rely upon Leqing Baoguan Temple to renounce the world. Later, he visited Yuansou, who said, "Does it come from the eastern ridge?
Does it come from the western ridge? The Master pointed to his straw sandals and said, "These were bought for three copper coins. Yuansou said, "Not yet."
He spoke further. The Master said, "I am just like this; what about you, Preceptor? The Old Man said, "Out of consideration for you being a newcomer, I grant you thirty blows.

The Master then realized the essential meaning. After some time, having thoroughly exhausted the depths of the treasury, he said, "As soon as one involves discursive thought, it all becomes superfluous dharma.
He first resided at Wufeng in Ningbo. In the fifth year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued to establish a Buddhist assembly.
At Mount Zhong, he summoned a śramaṇa of noble conduct; Master [Zhao] and Master Le Jitan were among those present.
Later, while residing at Lingyin, he ascended the hall and cited Master Xiangyan, saying: "Last year’s poverty was not yet true poverty; this year’s poverty is only then true poverty."
"Last year I was poor, yet I still had enough ground to set my awl upon; this year I am so poor that I do not even have an awl.

Suddenly, a man from among the assembly stepped forward and asked, "Venerable sir, you are mistaken. Today is the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha’s birthday. How can you cite this public case?
The mountain monk simply replied, "The duties of the abbot are many. [This was said] during the formal lecture on bathing the Buddha, citing Yaoshan.
When Zen Master Yan was bathing the Buddha with Zun Bunan, Mount Yaoshan asked him, "You have bathed this one;
can you also bathe that one? Zun said, "Bring me that one. Yaoshan then desisted. The Master [Yunmen] said:
"This one and that one—each and every one has been bathed from the very beginning. Yaoshan and Bunan were merely engaging in idle deliberation; look closely at this!"
"Forming a falling conversation. Forming a falling conversation. About to bring about confusion. [The Master] struck the meditation seat and said: "The spring in Wulin has already grown old;
the terraces and pavilions are filled with lush green shade. In his room, the Master gave a vertical statement (chuyu), saying:

"The Lotus Peak has been eaten away by woodworms on one side. Why do you not know? He further said: "I shall not ask about Cold Spring Pavilion swallowing Upheaval Pavilion; what about South High Peak?"
"Competing for the forehead with North Peak"—this was his [the Master's] "seventh mechanism. In the nineteenth year, he encountered an unexpected calamity and was arrested.

Some advised the Master to plan for his own safety early on, but he paid them no heed. With a serene countenance, he went to the authorities; before the interrogation had even begun, he recited a gāthā beneath the corridor eaves and passed away while sitting upright.
Chan Master Fanchi Chu-shih of T'ien-ning Monastery in Hai-yen Prefecture was the son of the Zhu family of Shang-mang, Ning-po.

From the time he was in his swaddling clothes, a monk saw him and said to his father, "This is the Sun of the Buddha; he will surely cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish and illuminate this turbid world.
At nine years of age, he was taught the scriptures; at sixteen, he became a monk; and at twenty, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage on "conditions and seeing" (*yuan-jian*).

Because of light and darkness, "non-seeing" is established; yet when there is no light, it is not [non-seeing]. If one’s own nature were to manifest, then all appearances of darkness could never obscure it.
Having gained an awakening to this, he went to visit Yuan-sou at Mount Jing and asked: "What is meant by 'the utterance is not sound, and that which precedes form is not an object'?"
The old man suddenly said, "When words are uttered, they are not sound; when colors appear before one, they are not objects. Speak quickly! Speak quickly!

As the Master was about to offer a reply, the old man let out a thunderous shout. The Master was struck with confusion and withdrew. Later, while selected for the project of transcribing the Great Canon, he arrived at Chongtian Gate in the capital.
One night, hearing the sound of drums atop a decorated tower, he attained sudden and great enlightenment. He composed a verse, beginning: "Chong..."
Outside the Heavenly Gate, the drums thunder; suddenly, the void collapses upon the earth. Shidi picks up a flake of snow from a red furnace; it is but the ice of the Yellow River in the sixth month.
Returning for winter retreat, he again visits the Elder. The Elder welcomes him with a smile and says, "I am glad that the great matter is now complete.
He orders him to share his seat. Not long after, he enters the world at Fuzhen in Haiyan, followed by Baoguo, and subsequently moves to his own monastery.

He was awakened. The Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the honorary title of Chan Master Furi Puzhao Hui bian (Sun Illumining Everywhere, Wisdom and Eloquence). In the year Dingyou, he presided over Tianning Monastery in the prefecture.
On the day he opened the hall for his inaugural sermon, a monk asked: "I am originally without a mind that seeks anything;
now this great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously. What is this great treasure of the Dharma King? The Master said: "Those with eyes see it; those with ears hear it."
[The Master] said, "There is none who honors [the truth]; it is just this. The Teacher said, "Shatter the skull and pull out the nostrils.
[The monk] asked, "How is it to be used? The Teacher said, "Just wait until the rain soaks your head. He ascended the hall and raised the case:
A monk asked Qianfeng, "The *Bhagavāns* of the ten directions all share the single path to Nirvana; I wonder where the beginning of that path lies? Qianfeng drew a line with his staff.
Huai said, "It is right here. The Master said, "Ten thousand miles of white clouds. The monk recounted the previous dialogue and asked Yunmen about it.
Yunmen said, "The fan leaps up to the thirty-third heaven, striking the nose of Śakra; a carp from the Eastern Sea is struck with a blow, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin.
The Master said, "Ten thousand miles of white clouds. Suppose someone were to come out and ask, 'Tianning...'"
With such a critique, do you still satisfy the intent of those two great elders? To them he said: "Ten thousand miles of white clouds—ha ha ha!
La la li, la la li! In every land and every dust mote, how many are there? At the crossroads stands the Stone Daring One;
suddenly he sucks dry the waters of the vast ocean. You lot, you eggplants and gourds, where would you know this? *Clap!*
He rose from his meditation seat and ascended the hall. He recited: "The Superior Man of Shang, Qiu Yi Ji, transformed three thousand seventy scholars.

You, little students, eight or nine sons, compose fine benevolence; you may know propriety. He called to the assembly, saying: "What kind of speech is this? None of the disciples of Confucius recognized it;
the blue-eyed barbarian monk smiles and nods his head. Ascending the hall again, he said: "All of you, do you see?"
When I open my mouth, you immediately take it as a discourse on the Dharma; when you see me remain silent, you immediately take it as a meeting in silence.
You all seek me at both extremes; how could you know that I am not at either extreme? Tell me, where do you usually find me?
Is it standing atop a high peak, yet not revealing the crown of his head? Or is it walking upon the bottom of the deep sea, yet his feet remain dry? If it were like this—
He has already been found by him. Do you know that this mountain monk possesses a secret formula for hiding the body? "All day long one does not see him, yet one sees him constantly;
throughout the entire day they meet, yet they do not meet. "Where there is thought, it is entirely a prison of affliction; where there is no mind, it is truly a crystal palace.
(He gives a shout. Ascending the hall: Upon hearing the signal for tea, go drink tea; upon hearing the signal for bathing, go bathe.
Hearing the Way of Mount Shou, you all should "rest" and "cease. Why do you not consent to go in this manner?
Suddenly, if someone were to come forth and say, "Venerable Sir, I cannot blame you," you would tell him: "Before you even reached Mount Shou, I have already given you thirty blows!
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings are much like a cesspool. You...
"Why do you pointlessly thrust your head inside? Come, come; I shall engage you in some idle talk.
He took up his staff and said, "As for the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and the old monks throughout the world, when they arrive here, their wits are blunted and their tongues are tied.

Try to say something! The assembly was at a loss. The Master said, "You have been deceived to death. He ascended the hall and said, "For a long time I have sat facing the wall; the Way is cut off and men are scarce."
Constantly pressing forward, with eyes twitching and ears burning, there has never been one who travels far without stopping, nor one who stays long without moving.
At times, he raises his staff at the crossroads, blending his light with the radiance and sharing his dust with the world;
truly, he proceeds with brilliant splendor in every place. At other times, atop a solitary peak, he sets down his alms-bowl bag and shuts himself away.
Block the ravine and seal its opening. Blaze forth in every direction, letting all things wither into stillness. To say "this very mind is Buddha" is not permitted;
to say "neither mind nor Buddha" is not permitted; to say "not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing" is also not permitted.
"I see two clay oxen fighting their way into the sea; until this very day, there has been no news. (He lets out a shout.
One day, because a donor had presented him with *yangmei* (cherries), a monk picked one up from the box and asked, "These *yangmei* are all the same;
why are some red and some white? The Master closed the lid of the box and said, "What have you seen? The monk was speechless. (Qingshan)

Dai [the monk] immediately turned the box over and said, "I request the Master to examine it. The Master opened the box again and said, "What? The monk remained speechless. (Qingshan’s substitute says: "Whether you use red or white, it is fine.
The Master said, "You are simply a fellow who knows nothing of opening and closing. He asked, "For what purpose does the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion employ so many hands and eyes?
The Master said, "The spring breeze does not wrap its head. One evening, while gazing at the moon, a monk pointed...
Yue asked the Master, "One half is so bright; why is this other half so dark? The Master said, "As for the bright, let it be bright; as for the dark, let it be dark.
Yue asked, "On the fifteenth night, when it is full, where does the darkness go? The Master said, "I would give you thirty blows for that, and it would not be too much.
Yue said, "In that case, there is neither brightness nor darkness at all. The Master— [said: "... (The Master remained silent).
[The Master] asked, "Did you see the true moon? The monk said, "What is the true moon? The Master said, "It does not illuminate. The monk asked, "What is it like when it illuminates?
The Master said, "How many people are there who reach for the sky and trace the earth? The monk asked, "Is this not simply that very thing? The Master said, "This is still but a shadow.
As the monk was about to offer further words, the Master gave a shout. Another monk came forward offering a staff. The Master said, "From..."
"From where have you come? The monk held up his staff. The Master raised it and said, "Is this the essence (ti) or the function (yòng)?

The monk replied, "When grasping it, one gives rise to function from the essence; when letting go, one brings the function back into the essence. The Master said, "Coming as you do, you have obtained only its essence, not its function.
The monk said, "If the Master raises it thus, you have obtained only its function, not its essence. The Master struck the ground once with his staff.

[The Master] leaned on his staff and said: "Body and function are gathered together. On the eleventh day of the ninth month of the first year of Hongwu, the Emperor summoned the Master to preach the Dharma at Jiangshan.

The court officials reported his discourse, and the Sovereign was greatly pleased. In the third month of the second year, following the precedent of the first year, the Emperor again summoned the Master to preach the Dharma as before.
A banquet was bestowed beneath the Wenlou Hall, where he personally received the Emperor's favor.
Question: When he returned, the Inner Treasury was opened and white silver was bestowed upon him.

In the autumn of the third year, the Emperor, considering that the principles of ghosts and spirits are profoundly obscure, felt that the scriptures must surely contain clear and subtle explanations. He therefore summoned those among the monks who were proficient in the teachings of the Tripiṭaka to question them.
The Master, along with sixteen others including Mengtang Xingzhong, responded to the summons and arrived. They were lodged at the Great [Monastery].

At Tianjie Temple, he was summoned by imperial decree to receive honors from the Ministry of Rites. Subsequently, he drew upon the sūtras and śāstras to compose a treatise, intending to enter the court to present it for deliberation.
Suddenly, manifesting slight illness, he sat in the full lotus posture and wrote a verse, saying: "The true nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, there is neither birth nor extinction."
A wooden horse neighed at night, and the sun rose from the west. When he finished writing his final testament, he said to Mengtang, "Brother, I am about to depart.
Tang asked, "Where will you go? The Master replied, "I am going to the West. Tang asked, "The Buddha is in the West; is there no Buddha in the East?
The Master let out a thunderous roar and passed away. This was on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month. His disciples then received his遗 (yi) [final instructions].
His remains and those parts that did not decay were returned to sea salt. His stupa was located at Xizhi. He was seventy-five years of age and had been a monk for sixty-two years.
Chan Master Yuguan Zhiji of Jingshan in Hangzhou was the son of the Gu family of Wuxian County in Suzhou; he was born with spiritual endowments.

His origins were extraordinary. Upon entering Haiyun Monastery as a youth, he studied both Buddhist scriptures and Confucian classics with equal diligence, earning the admiration of his teacher, who ordained him by shaving his head and bestowing upon him the full precepts.
Hearing that the master Xianshou was lecturing on the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, he went to listen.

Before the chapter had even concluded, he smiled broadly and said: "The single true *dharmadhātu* is perfectly identical to the vast void; yet, as soon as it involves words and phrases, it is no longer so."
"This is merely a matter of surplus. Even if one were to obtain a rain of jeweled flowers from heaven, what benefit would that be to me? Thereupon, he went to Jianye to visit Xiaoyin at Longxiang.
Xiaoyin was one whose literary talent and moral virtue moved the entire world; the Master subtly revealed his own literary brilliance, and they mutually praised one another.
A fellow practitioner, the Senior Seat-holder Yu, rebuked him, saying: "Your talent is so exceptionally brilliant; do you not think of taking up the burden [of the Dharma]?"
"Is the Great Dharma merely the servant of poems and *sao* lyrics? What understanding do you have of the verse by Wujindeng that speaks of 'yellow leaves fluttering'?
The Master was silenced and unable to offer a reply; he returned to Haiyun and did not close his eyes for over a month.
Suddenly, seeing autumn leaves falling in the courtyard, he attained a sudden realization. He then went to visit Yuansou at Jing.

[The Master] Shan subsequently attained the Dharma from him. In the *Renwu* year of the *Zheng* era (1362), the Xuanzheng Yuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) nominated the Master to take up the abbacy at Longjiao Temple in Changguo.
Upon ascending the hall, the Master called out to the assembly; the assembly all looked up at him. The Master said, "A hawk flies over Silla," and immediately descended from the seat.
Upon ascending the hall again, a monk asked: "Śākyamuni has already passed away, and Maitreya has not yet been born. At this very moment, who is the one entrusted with the Buddha-Dharma?"

"To whom should it be entrusted? The Master said, "I, this old monk, beat the drum of retreat. [The student] asked, "With no Śākyamuni before and no Maitreya behind, is there still a portion for study?
The Master said, "The wind does not come; the tree does not move. He then said, "Before one's eyes, there is no dharma."
Outside the mind there are no phenomena; the imperial wind sweeps vast and wide, and the people and all things flourish in harmony.

Flowers fall in profusion; the sun lingers long. High and low, the mountain ridges and valleys are encircled by brocade. One wonders why, at that time, the cuckoo—amidst the boundless beauty of the spring mountains—still cried out, "It is not as good as returning home.
Ascending the hall: It is now the third month, the season of Qingming. Neither cold nor hot, half-shaded and half-sunny.
"Falling petals, crying birds—one sound after another. Suddenly he seized his staff and said: "He pierces the nostrils of Heshang Xuanze; he blinds the eyes of Bodhidharma.

The Teaching: A single phrase encompasses all. A three-legged donkey prances about on its hooves; ten thousand miles, not a blade of grass. Entering the hall, he said:
"The four great elements are fundamentally empty—upon what does the Buddha rely to abide? The lush green bamboo is entirely the Dharma-body.

now that the letter from Elder Tong of Shanguan, the successor, has arrived. Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "Since the time of chaotic confusion, for thirty years there has been no lack of salt and sauce.
Only after the snowfall does one know the integrity of the pine and cypress. Let you be as you are—neither mind nor Buddha—I simply maintain this."
"The mind is itself the Buddha. Only when things are difficult does one truly see the mind of a man of great capacity.
Some say, "The news from Jiangxi has been communicated," or "The plum on Daming Mountain has ripened. Such skillful means (*upāya*) of Shanguan must indeed be like this.
But as for Shitou’s saying, "The letter does not arrive, and the message does not pass"—how will you all explain this? If you can speak directly right now, you will have the adze.
[The Master] had not yet arrived when he was there. One day, as the Master entered the garden, he saw the head cook cutting melons.
The Master asked, "How many patriarchs' heads have you cut? The cook replied, "Thirty. The Master said, "Which of these has blood beneath the skin?
The cook said, "Why do you, Reverend, mock me so repeatedly? The Master said, "A good heart does not receive a good reward. A monk asked, "What is purity?"

The Master said: "If you wish to avoid being too late, you must go to the place where there is no 'too late'. The monk bowed. The Master said: "You have already been too late. The monk asked: "What about the time before the ox was born? The Master said: "The ox has already been born. The monk asked: "What about the ox itself? The Master said: "The ox has already been born. The monk asked: "What about the young? The Master said: "The young has already been born. The monk asked: "What about the mother? The Master said: "The mother has already been born. [The monk said: "It was just that the Master did not speak. Shan called for an attendant to bring a lamp, whereupon the monk withdrew and returned to the assembly.

What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "A pair of mandarin ducks cannot be painted. [The monk] asked: "The mind of the Great Sage of the Land of Chu (India) was secretly transmitted from east to west.
What is this mind of secret transmission? The Master said: "In the ninth month, golden leaves fall in profusion."
[The monk] said, "Preceptor, do not point to external objects for people. The Master said, "This old monk has committed a transgression.

[The monk] asked, "There is no Maitreya in heaven, and there is no Maitreya under the earth. I wonder, who gave him his name? The Master said, "I am walking through the wild weeds; you, moreover, have entered a deep village.
[The monk] asked, "The body of the Pure Dharma-realm fundamentally has neither appearance nor disappearance. For what reason did Śākyamuni today..."

[The Master] descended [into the world]. The Teacher said, "To know and yet deliberately transgress. [Nanquan] Zunbu said, "While Zun was bathing the Buddha, Yaoshan asked him, 'You can only bathe this one;
can you also bathe that one? Zun replied, 'Bring me that one. [Yaoshan asked,] 'What is that one?
The Teacher said, 'Carrying the cangue and passing through the legal proceedings. [The monk] asked, "What is the original body of Vairocana? The Teacher said, "Not apart from it."
The disciple asked, "How does one maintain [this state]? The Master said, "He has no sores himself; do not wound him.
The disciple asked, "What is it that within a single phrase contains the three mysteries? The Master said, "Driving an iron boat atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak.
The disciple asked, "What is it that within a single mystery contains the three essentials? The Master said, "The pupils in the eyes blow wood-horns and shout. The disciple asked, "How..."
"This is the family style of our Preceptor," [the student] said. The Master replied, "It blows down the pine tree in front of the gate. [The student] said, "I am not asking about this wind.
The Master asked, "What wind are you asking about? [The student] said, "The family style. The Master said, "In my place, great merit is not rewarded.
[The student] asked, "Since it is the one true Dharma-realm, why are there ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences? The Master said:
"The sweet melon is sweet to its very stem; the bitter gourd is bitter to its very root. [The student] asked: "Is the Way far? It is real upon contact with things.
What do you call 'real'? The Master said: "A thousand-year-old tree that casts no shadow. [The student] said: "Are the sages far? Embody them and they are divine."

"What do you call 'divinity'? The Master said, "A bottomless whip of these times. [The monk] asked, "At the moment when the multitude of yin is about to depart but has not yet departed, and when the single yang is about to arise but has not yet arisen—is there still Buddha-dharma or not?

The Master said, "The bell rings as a bell; the drum sounds as a drum. [The monk] said, "From ancient times to the present, it has never fallen away; it is clearly before one's eyes. The Master said, "Do not look with your eyes."
Hua. In the *guichou* year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict summoned ten eminent monks to the Tianjie Temple in the capital;
the Master was indeed at their head. Due to illness, he was unable to attend the audience. In the *yimao* year, he was granted leave to return to Haeun.

On the eighth day of the eighth month in the *wumu* year, he suddenly manifested slight illness. On the fourth day of the ninth month, he took up his brush to write a verse and passed away. His disciples...
He divided his fingernails and hair to enshrine at Mount Jing.
Chan Master Xingzhong Zhiren of Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou Prefecture was the son of the Wu family of Fanyang in Rao.
From childhood, his insight was exceptionally sharp. He studied under Yuansou, who said, "Ren Shuji is one who possesses the wings of a tiger. He subsequently emerged into the world [to teach].
He visited temples such as Dezhang, Chongbao, and Wanshou. Taking leave of Wanshou, he returned to Songlin and addressed the assembly:

"This illusory body is approaching the age of eighty; I shall walk beneath the pines and sleep upon the rocks. Take care, O assembly of dragons and elephants of the Northern Mountains! When will the discourse of the Putong era reach its completion?
At the beginning of the Hongwu era, the Emperor questioned him regarding the principles of ghosts and spirits; the Master explained them according to the Buddha’s intent.
He recorded this and presented it [to the Emperor], who was greatly pleased. At the time of his death, he wrote a verse and passed away.
Chan Master Tianjing Yuanjing of Tiantai Monastery in Shaoxing Prefecture was the son of the Ni family of Kuaiji in Yue. He ascended the hall and said:
"Mind itself is Buddha. A cow in Jia Prefecture eats the grain. "Neither mind nor Buddha. A horse in Yi Prefecture has a bloated belly. "Not mind, not Buddha.
Seeking a physician throughout the world, one applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig. After a long while, he said: "To cry until the blood flows is of no use;
it is better to keep one's mouth shut and pass through the remainder of spring. He ascended the hall and said: "Sound is not sound—this is Avalokiteśvara."
Obscure. Form is not form; this is the Dharma-gate of Mañjuśrī. Sound and form are unimpeded; this is the realm of Samantabhadra. Holding up his staff and drawing a line, he said:
"The great garuḍa spreads its wings, covering the ten continents; the swallows and sparrows by the hedge chirp in vain.

In the Ming Dynasty, an assembly was convened at Zhongshan Mountain, and the Master, along with Bifeng, were summoned into the inner palace. They conversed with ease regarding the Way. The ninth year of Hongwu.
He served as the abbot of Lingyin Monastery. Having been unjustly exiled to Shaanxi, he stayed overnight at Ningguo Temple in Baoying and passed away while sitting upright.
Chan Master Mengtang Tanne of Guoqing Monastery in Taizhou was the son of the Wang family of Cixi; both his grandfather and father held official posts.

By his late years, he had exhaustively surveyed the Confucian classics and penetrated their essential meaning. He once sighed, saying: "Toiling over books and refining rhetoric are merely worldly phenomena;
why not seek the supramundane Dharma? He went to consult Yuanzou. Yuanzou’s demeanor was stern and severe; none who were not scholars of long-standing learning dared to even look upon his gate.
The Master stepped straight forward to inquire and seek instruction. Their spiritual sparks clashed, cutting off the paths of conceptual thought.
"Stop," the old man nodded in agreement. In the fifth year of the Zhizheng era, he emerged from seclusion at Baosheng Temple;

he was subsequently transferred to Kaishou and later to Guoqing, where he was bestowed the honorary title "Buddha Zhenwen Yidi. In the second year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict summoned monks of realized virtue, and the Master was among those selected.
Upon his audience with the Emperor, the Sovereign took pity on his advanced age and granted him leave to return to the mountains. One day, without prior illness, he addressed his younger brother...
The Master said: "The three realms are like flowers in the sky, swept away by the wind; the six objects of sense are like illusory shadows, like snow melted by boiling water.
From antiquity to the present, only this single nature remains alone. I shall now enter extinction; listen to my verse: "I have a thing, without head and without tail;
If you wish to see it clearly, look after nirvana. Having spoken these words, he sat upright and passed away.
Chan Master Guding Zuming of Mount Jing in Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of the Ying family of Yingcheng, Fencheng, Mingzhou. Initially, he visited Yuansou.
One day, while in the inner quarters, [Zuming] questioned him regarding the karmic conditions of Huanglong’s meeting with Ciming. Yuansou interrogated him, saying:
"As for Zhaozhou’s statement, 'The old woman at Mount Tai has been exposed by me,' Ciming laughed and asked: 'Was this a rebuke?'"
"Tell me, are these two old men alike in their gallbladders and livers, or are they different in their nostrils?
The Master said, "A pair of iron hammers without holes. The Old Man said, "If Huanglong had attained enlightenment at that moment, what would have happened?

The Master said, "A diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky. The Old Man said, "Not so, not so. As the Master was about to step forward, the Old Man gave a shout. From that time on, [the Master] was at ease.
He was unimpeded in his realization. While serving as the head of the scriptorium (jishi), he was inspired morning and evening, reaching ever deeper into the profound mysteries of the Dharma.

In the first year of the Yuantong era, he first departed from Mount Jing to reside at Longjiao in Changguo. He soon thereafter presided over Mount Jing, receiving the title Chan Master Huixing Wenmin Hongxue Puzhi.
When a monk asked, "What is the Buddha? the Master replied, "A weight dipped in vinegar. [The monk] asked, "What is..."
Regarding the matter of the Buddha’s upward direction, the Master said, "Looking up, one does not see the sky. The monk asked, "I recall a monk asking Yunmen, 'What is the Buddha?
and Yunmen replied, 'A dried-up shit-stick. What about that? The Master said, "Yunmen was not being kind-hearted.

The monk asked, "How far apart are a dried-up shit-stick and a weight for a scale dipped in vinegar? The Master said, "In the cauldron of boiling water, there is no place that is cold. The monk—[was struck].
He prepared to depart. The Master then gave a shout. One day, suffering from a slight illness, he wrote a verse: "Birth and death are the dull reality; the great void is pure and full.
For seventy-nine years, the cradle rope has snapped. He threw down his brush and passed away.
Chan Master Falin of Zhuanquan at Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou was the son of the Huang family of Ninghai, Taizhou. He went to visit Yuansou at Zhongtianzhi Temple.
Yuansou asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Tiantai. Yuansou asked, "Have you ever seen Hanshan and Shide?
The Master joined his palms and stepped forward, saying, "Today I have personally seen the Master. Yuansou said, "That is empty talk and deception."
Han entered the hall. While he was reading the scriptures, an old man asked, "Are you reading the scriptures? The Master replied, "Yes. The old man said, "With what do you read them?
The Master said, "I read them with my eyes. The old man held up his fist and said, "Why not say that you read them with this?

The Master said, "Put down your fist; with what will you read them then? The old man smiled. In the fourth year of the Zhizhi era, he presided over Lingyin Monastery and ascended the hall to give a discourse.
The Dharma is the eternal Dharma; the Way is the eternal Way. It breaks through the gateway of the face; though the point is reached, it is not yet attained.
Xuefeng, with his assembly of one thousand seven hundred virtuous teachers, spent morning and evening rolling only three wooden balls.
Zhaozhou, a venerable Chan master of seven hundred years, would say only "Go drink tea" upon seeing anyone. Zhongfeng, while residing at Jujian, saw only his brothers visiting him...
This is the procedure for the general incense offering during cold or warm seasons: one joins the palms.

"If you are a true son of the Golden-Haired Lion, even from three thousand miles away, you will certainly not be at fault. Entering the hall, the Master raised the story of Zhaozhou’s cassock and said:
"Although Zhaozhou skillfully wielded the Great Sword to cut off this monk’s tongue, he could not avoid exposing his own family’s disgrace. At Lingyin, it is not so. Suddenly, there is..."
A monk asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? The Master replied to him, "Today is as hot as yesterday. Ascending the hall, he said:
"This famous mountain of Lingyin within the jurisdiction of Old Hangzhou was first established during the Xianhe era of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Dharma Master Huirui was its founding patriarch. Today is the auspicious festival of Shangyuan, when lanterns are lit in all places. The administrative officials..."

"May each of you take care of yourselves as the wind extinguishes a candle. He then descended from his seat. On the second day of the second month in the fifteenth year of Zhizheng, he manifested illness.
He wrote a verse, saying: "Seventy-two years as a nail driven into empty space; the final phrase—unspeakable, unspeakable."
He then suddenly passed away.
Chan Master Fuyuan Fabao of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was the son of the Fang family of Ninghai in Taizhou.
He went to visit Yuansou, who asked, "Where have you recently come from? The Master replied, "Jingci. Yuansou asked, "What brings you here? The Master said, "I have long admired [you]."
The Master came specifically to pay his respects, as the reputation of the Abbot had reached him. The Old Man asked, "When Zhaozhou saw Nanquan, what did he do?

The Master replied, "He stood with his head touching the sky and his feet treading the earth. The Old Man asked, "What was it like after he saw him? The Master replied, "When hungry, he ate; when tired, he slept.
The Old Man said, "Where did you learn such empty talk? The Master replied, "Today I have seen the Abbot in person. The Old Man—
He nodded in agreement. He went out and took up residence at Dongshan. Ascending the hall, he said: "If you raise one, you cannot raise two; if you let one point pass, you fall into the second.
When the ancients spoke thus, they were truly like those who embrace their own plunder while crying out for injustice.
Dongshan is not so: if you raise two, you cannot raise one; if you let one point pass, you fall into the seventh. At this point, you must know there is a direction to follow.
"The one path above has finally been attained. [The Master asked: "What is this path that goes above? After a long silence, he said: "Do not linger by the green herbs of the cold crags;
sit amidst the white clouds, for the essence of the school is not subtle. At the beginning of the Hongwu era, a śramaṇa of eminent practice was summoned via imperial post.

The Master went to the capital and frequently entered the inner court to respond to inquiries. His answers pleased the Emperor, who retained him for three years before granting him leave to return. He resided twice at Jingde Monastery.
When Master Shanshan fell gravely ill one day, his attendant requested a verse. The Master rebuked him, saying, "I still have three years of life remaining.
It turned out exactly as he had said. On the day of his passing, he suddenly clapped his hands and cried, "A-he-he!
O assembly, what is this? Look at Yiji!"
Chan Master Xiaoyin Dayin of Longxiang in Jinling was a successor of Chan Master Xiyuan Xi. He was a native of the Chen family of Nanchang. He went to study under Huiji, who asked him:
"Huanglong received the essential instruction at Ledu Temple and led his disciples on a journey to travel afar; yet upon meeting Ciming, his spirit became despondent and his bearing lowly."
"Where does the fault lie? The Master said, "In a peach pit from a thousand years ago, what old kernel are you looking for?
On another day, he questioned him with the story of Baizhang’s wild fox: "Tell me, when one says 'not falling into cause and effect,' one falls into the body of a wild fox;
when one says 'not obscuring cause and effect,' one sheds the body of a wild fox. Wherein lies the point of benefit or harm? As the Master was about to answer, [Baizhang] gave a shout.
"Hai! With these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment. He entered the world at Wuhui in Wuxing, later moving to Fengshan, Tiantian, and Tianli.

In the year Jisi (1339), Emperor Wen established the former Qian Palace in Jinling as Longxiang Jiqing Temple and issued an edict for the Master to serve as its founding abbot. Entering the hall, he said:
"The World-Honored One Śākyamuni relinquished the Golden Wheel to ascend the rank of Buddha; today, His Majesty the Emperor ascends from the rank of Buddha to govern the Golden [Wheel]."
The wheel gathers and encompasses the ocean of three thousand worlds within a single seal; it fully possesses eighty thousand dharma-gates upon a single hair-tip.

It is like the Bodhisattvas at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, who attained the liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit, producing various delicious foods and leftovers from a single vessel.
Furthermore, as the assembly looked up into the sky, it rained down various [seeds].
Various precious jewels satisfy the hearts of all sentient beings according to their inclinations. Thereafter, those who obtain these jewels shall fully realize the Dharma-gates;
those who taste their flavor shall all achieve the wondrous Way. There is not a single speck of dust that does not fully embody the Buddha-work;
there is not a single dharma that does not perfectly fulfill the True Teaching. Thus, we now construct this jewel monastery to propagate the gift of the Dharma. The voices of the devas...
Music played without being struck resonates of its own accord; the chanting of Brahma-songs and hymns unfolds naturally.

Bodhisattvas from the ten directions all assemble at the site of enlightenment, and the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, join in celebration and praise. Is there anyone who, without passing through the illusory city, proceeds directly to the precious destination?
Striking the whisk, he said: "The four seas have already come under the imperial transformation; in these times of peace, let us sing the song of Great Tranquility. (Text)
On the occasion of the full-term memorial service for the Imperial Ancestral Founder’s sacred anniversary, the Tripitaka was being recited. He ascended the hall and said:

"Venerable and unsurpassed, he transcends the primordial state before the Celestial Emperor; noble beyond naming, he sits firmly atop the summit of the ghostly mountain. As vast as that summit is, it encompasses and contains the ten voids."
In its vast application, it encompasses all categories of existence. It is like the moon reflected in myriad waters, making no distinction between the pure and the defiled;
or like springtime among a hundred flowers, wherein no signs of partiality or bias are seen. It is wondrous existence that is not existent, and true emptiness that is not empty. Thus it is said:
"The realms of boundless lands do not separate self and other by even a hair’s breadth; ten eons of past and present do not depart from the beginning and the end."
In a single thought-moment, one casts the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters and contains Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed.
In this very seeing, one encounters Emperor Wenzong. Formerly descending from the Buddha-ground to manifest in the royal palace, he governed the state and secured the ancestral altars;
once his work of transformation was complete, he returned to the rank of Buddha. His quiescent, unmoving wisdom universally responds throughout the ten directions, vast and open.
Your impartial transformation has already pervaded the sands of all worlds. Longxiong offers such praise; tell me, does this accord with the Sage’s intention?
After a long silence, he said: "The *utpala* flower blows on without ceasing; again it descends from Tuṣita to Jambudvīpa."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Words are uttered, yet they are not sound; forms appear before us, yet they are not objects. What is the reason for this attachment?
To sleep amidst sounds and forms, to sit and lie down amidst sounds and forms—this is already a step forward. Therefore it is said: 'This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing;

there are no further sounds or forms to present to you. If one understands this point, there is nothing at all; how could the distinction between essence and function hinder you? He then stepped off abruptly.
He held up his staff and said, "The flowing water carries yellow leaves; where does the ox that bears the cold come from? A crow flies past another village. He struck the ground with his staff.
He passed away on the fifth month of the Jia-shen year of the Zheng-tong era.
Chan Master Zhongfang Tianlun of Baoning in Jinling was the son of the Zhang family of Xiangshan in Mingzhou. He went to attend upon Huiji.
Huiji asked, "The lake mountains are lush and the lake waters flow wide; they soak your nostrils and block your eyes. Why do you not know [this]?
The Master replied, "Throughout my entire being there is no shadow or form; at every step, all traces of movement are cut off. Huiji said, "Not yet."

While on the way to visit Master [Huiji], the Master [Dongshan] shook his sleeves and departed. He subsequently stayed beneath the master’s seat and repeatedly questioned him about this matter, yet the master never spoke of it.
Thereupon, he went to Taohuawu in Wuxing and built a thatched hut. One day, hearing a clap of thunder, he attained realization and thoroughly saw through Huiji’s point of application.
He later appeared in the world at Dongquan, Foyan, and Baoning. On the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ascended the hall and said: "Last night, I saw the morning star."
Awakening to the Way: In the back garden, the wind blows down the fence; at dawn, there is no trace left to pursue. On the Snowy Mountains, the green grass grows as before.
Ascending the hall [to preach], he said: "The third and the eleventh; the ninth and the seventh. Seven times nine is sixty-three; nine times nine is eighty-one.
In the morning one departs for the Western Heaven, in the evening one returns to the land of Tang. One horse gives birth to three tigers; the stone ox guards the ancient gate."
The Road. [He] entered the hall for the formal discourse: "The teachings of the Sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon.
Yesterday someone came from West State, bringing news from East State, reporting that a man from the kingdom of Tājika is selling medicinal incense upon his eyelashes.
[He] gave a shout.
Chan Master Zhengkui of the First Monastery of Zhongtianzhi in Hangzhou was the son of the Fang family of Poyang in Rao.
He went to attend on Huiji, who asked him, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "From Poyang. Huiji asked, "How deep is the water in Lake Poyang?"
The Master said, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one does not see the bottom. Jiji said, "If that is so, then even the nostrils of a patch-robed monk will be soaked and rotted away.
The Master said, "I certainly do not borrow the Venerable’s nostrils to breathe. Jiji asked, "In the end, whose nostrils do you borrow to breathe?"
The Master said, "I respectfully wish the Abbot ten thousand blessings. Ji approved of this. Later, while presiding over the assembly, he instructed them: "Mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way.
A single thought involving deliberation causes the whole body to enter the weeds. Therefore it is said: 'Before one's eyes there is no dharma.'"
The intent lies before one’s eyes, yet it is not the dharma of the present moment; it is not something reached by the ears or the eyes.

The heavens and earth of past and present, the sun and moon of past and present, the mountains and rivers of past and present, and the human relations of past and present—all are manifest in every instance and fully revealed in every thing.

It is not borrowed from the thousand sages, nor sought through the myriad functions. Within and without, there is nothing to take up; throughout past and present, there is no fixed location. Thus it is.
"How can you understand this? You are still mistaking the bridge of a donkey's saddle for your father’s chin.
Nevertheless, since he is the Great Saint of Sizhou, why did he appear in Yangzhou? After a long silence, he said, "Investigate!"

Chan Master Zuying of the Stone Chamber at Yuwang in Mingzhou was the son of the Chen family in Wujiang, Suzhou. Having left home at the age of seven, he immediately took up his staff to travel among the teachers.
Upon hearing of the spiritual transformation of Huiji, he went to join him with great urgency; upon their first meeting, they reached a state of mutual accord.

He subsequently emerged from seclusion to reside at Longgui and then at Yuwang. In response to the request of Chan Master Pingshi Dizhi to offer a verse on his illness, he said: "This body is without self, yet it is ill."

The roots run deep. As Mañjuśrī visits from afar with a sense of shame, the mountain flowers themselves discourse on non-duality. Facing each other before the blue lamp, they laugh and chant with joyful smiles.
At the time of his passing, he addressed the assembly, saying: "For fifty-three years I have played at being clever only to end up clumsy; I have trodden through empty space and walk barefoot.
The myriad phenomena and all living beings cannot help but laugh until their hearts ache."

Chan Master Meiwu Nianchang of Xiangfu Temple in Jiaxing Prefecture was originally from Huating. His surname was Huang. At the age of twelve, he received the tonsure at Yuanming Monastery in Pingjiang.
