Without deploying a single blade, one must overcome the enemy with the full edge of one's prowess. If it is not yet so—if you hesitate or fail to respond—your skull will shatter into pieces.
He planted his staff upright, gave a shout, and descended from the seat. While on a boat, he encountered the winter solstice.
Small Lecture: A single path of empty luminosity is entirely one’s own field. Since the first hexagram-line has already manifested its omen, it fully reveals that which transcends kalpas.
Within heaven and earth, there is no distinction between coming and going, movement and stillness; there is no difference between acceptance and rejection, right and wrong.
One may ride upon sound and cover over form; one may flow along with the current. One may sail the half-leaf boat on the Huating River, and one may exhaust...
In this land of marshes and misty waves, one does not raise the hook of Ren Gong; it is no different from the excursion upon the Hao River. Striking the whisk, he said:
"A single stroke across the mouth has already spoiled the salt and vinegar; three inches off the hook—do not look back. Tapping his knee, he said:
"The moon shines bright through the night as the heavens reflect in the water; the cry of wild geese flies past the floating islet of *ping*. He asked: "The bitter cold of mid-winter—"
[The monk asked: "Year after year, the affairs of the world proceed; how does the movement of the sun's shadow shift? The Master said: "Last night the sun’s orb drifted away with its cassia blossoms;
this morning in the moon’s cave, *zhicao* mushrooms have sprouted. [The monk] asked: "The direct transmission has already transcended the subtle and the manifest (*liwei*).

Having cut off all manifold distinctions, I ask you, Master, to provide an answer. The Master said: "A broken mirror does not reflect again; fallen flowers are difficult to support back up. [The monk] said: "If I go on just like this..."

"How is it now? The Master said, "A tortoise drilling through a ruined wall. The questioner asked, "If preaching the Dharma does not accord with the capacity [of the listener], it is all untimely speech.
How can one preach so as to accord with the capacity? The Master said, "Rising at midnight, one loses the ox;
rising at dawn, one loses the fire. The questioner asked, "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. Is this truly so? The Master said:
"Eating food stops hunger; drinking water stops thirst. He said, "Where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly avoid speaking of it.
But how about this? The Master replied, "Block your ears and listen clearly. On the eighth month of the Gui-mao year, he passed away.
Chan Master Shian Mao of Qingliang Temple in Ruizun, Mingzhou, was the son of the Zheng family of Fenghua in the commandery.

While still a child, he would sit in meditation during the middle of the night; his mother detested this and would push him over, yet he would invariably remain awake until dawn. Later, he left home to study under Chan Master Nanjian Quan.
One night, beneath the moonlight on the pines, he attained realization upon hearing the sound of flowing water. He went to inform Master Quan of his insight. Quan said:
He was sent to Gulin. Gulin asked, "Why have you come? The Master replied, "Precisely because the matter of birth and death is great, I have come to seek liberation.
Gulin said, "You clearly know that the four elements and five aggregates are the root of birth and death; why then have you entered this leather bag?
As the Master hesitated, Gulin struck him with his monk's staff, whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment. In the *Zheng* year *Renwu*, he took up residence there.
At Mount Ruiyun of Changming, there was a monk who had not yet finished his dialogue with the Master when he struck the ground with his hand and laughed.
The Master said, "Why must you bring out such stale merchandise? The monk let out a single sigh, and the Master then gave a shout.

The monk attained realization and withdrew to live in seclusion at Dongtang, never venturing beyond the mountains. Yuanming, the Master’s own disciple, invited him back to Cixuan at Tiantong; not long after, [the Master passed away].
He manifested illness. When the assembly requested that he write a verse, the Master said, "Within this, I am vast and empty; what need is there for a verse?
He then sat upright, leaning against a couch, clenched his right hand into a fist, and rested his forehead upon it, passing away. He was posthumously titled Great Chan Master Fuguang Puzhao.

Chan Master Jinglin Jìng of Mount Jìngshān in Hángzhōu was a successor of Chan Master Línghǐn Hǎi. A native of the region, he was exceptionally gifted from his youth and entered the monastic order at a tender age.

He frequently sought instruction from renowned masters, who directed him to investigate the "original person. After a long period, he attained realization and composed a verse, saying: "The original person, the original person—there is none..."
The brain has no head; how can one seek it? Suddenly, he seized the other’s nostril and said, “Look! It is originally just a commoner.
The other squinted his eyes and said, “Is that so? The Master gave him a slap.
Chan Master Daguizhengzhang of Mount Doufeng in Jianning Prefecture was a native of Fucheng, Fuzhou. He received the tonsure under Jueting of Hunan.
Later, he studied under Dongyu Hai and, upon hearing Hai’s verse on the story of Zhizhi pointing his finger, attained sudden enlightenment.

He immediately went to the abbot’s quarters to present his realization. Dongyu asked, “What is it? The Master replied, “A matter already perfected throughout past and present; why must one involve oneself in [conceptualization]?”
Haishan said, "If you do not engage in thought, how have you come here? The Master said, "I ask the Master to bear witness. Haishan said, "Witness what? The Master then gave a shout.

Haishan had him compose a verse on the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature. The Master said: A wooden dog has no Buddha-nature; Even if one seeks it for a thousand years, it cannot be found. If you wish to know its true form, Look at the face of the old woman selling cakes.
"The dog has no Buddha-nature; look at it and its eyes wither. In a flash, it turns over—Oṃ Śrī Sulu. He then sealed this with the *hai-fu* mudrā.

Later, he built a thatched hut on Mount Doufeng, which gradually developed into a monastic community. Entering the hall for a discourse, after a long silence, he said: "Though gold is precious, once it enters the eye, it becomes but dust.
He then descended from the seat. Entering the hall again, he said: "The jade palace is clear with frost; the emerald groves shed their leaves."
Holding it up entirely and exclusively, the myriad functions of the mind have been gradually eroded. Those who act as masters love to seek out medicine for those who are ill.
Entering the hall, he raised the story of the "Qingzhou Cloth Shirt" and said: "In the third watch of last night, the rain soaked the void; did the tabby cat know it or not?"
He climbed up and stood upon the treetop. Entering the hall, he said: "The beginning of the New Year brings forth prosperity; all things flourish.
To call this 'the start of the new year' is to blind your eyes with the Buddha-dharma. Not to call it 'the start of the new year' is to break my own tongue with the Buddha-dharma.
Ultimately, what is it? He then descended from his seat. His verse at the time of death says: "Birth is fundamentally not born; cessation is likewise without ceasing. It is an illusion."
"Departure and arrival—what need is there for discrimination? The great assembly, take heed: it does not reside in words. Having spoken thus, he joined his palms and entered *nirvāṇa*.
Chan Master Dàqiān Huìzhào, the Great King of Nurturing (Yùwáng), of Mingzhou, was the son of the Mǎ family of Yǒngjiā.
He first visited Huìméi, and subsequently visited Dōngyǔ at Jiànyán in Sū. Dōngyǔ asked him, "Rushing east and running west, what do you intend to do? The Master replied:
"I have come specifically to pay my respects to you," [the Master] said. Yunyu replied, "The heavens have no four walls and the earth extends beyond the eight frontiers;
on what ground do you place your feet? The Master struck his palms together upon the table and withdrew. Later, when Yunyu moved to Jingci Temple, he invited the Master to share the seat with him.

In the Wuchen year of the Tianli era, the Master took charge at Mingqing in Leqing. He addressed the assembly, saying: "If you wish for the Buddha-dharma to manifest before you, do not harbor the notion of knowing."
[The Master] replied: "To understand, to untie [the knots], to practice dhyāna, and to study the teachings—all these are inevitably obstacles.

How can one compare this to the state where not a single thing is established, yet one moves and dwells with complete freedom? This is why Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout were also used out of sheer necessity.

In the year Yiwu of the Zhi Zheng era, he moved to Putuo. Not long after, he was appointed to the position of Acting Abbot at Yuyang. He once offered three "critical barriers" (*san guan*) to instruct his students, saying:
The fierce tiger in the mountains takes flesh as its life; for what reason does it not eat its own offspring? Space has no front or back;
by what cause do there exist east, west, south, and north? [A being] has drunk milk equal to the four great oceans, and the bones accumulated are like Mount Vipula.

Who were your original parents? He lived there for nine years, then retired to Miaoxi. He built a cottage by a spring called Meng’an (Dream Hermitage) and remained there in solitary seclusion behind closed doors.
He paid no heed even as layers of dust accumulated on his mats. In the sixth year of the Hongwu era, he passed away.
The laywoman Sankong was among the most virtuous disciples of Chan Master Tantan of Tianning. Possessing the resolve of a heroic man, she was not swayed by wealth or status.
She studied under Zhuyun, who instructed her to single-mindedly uphold the "Mu" (No) koan. In this manner, thirty-six years passed. One day, she suddenly asked:
"When birth and death arrive, what then? Yun said, "Who is it that is born? Who is it that dies? The layman bowed his head in greeting.
Yun, suspecting him of being extraordinary, pressed him further, saying, "Who is it that gives birth?
Who is it that dies? The layman again bowed his head in greeting. Yun said, "Be careful not to die right here. The layman picked up his prayer beads and counted them.
He possessed one hundred and eight prayer beads. After several days, he manifested a slight illness, spoke a verse, and passed away. Following the cremation, countless śarīras were obtained.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Zhuyuan Zhen.
Chan Master Tanzang Zhong of Mount Jian in Jinling was a native of Nankang. When the Prince of Liang arrived at Jiankang, that very night the temple was destroyed by fire.
The next day, the Prince went to the temple and asked, "How shall we restore it? The Master replied, "We rely on the presence of a great donor."

The King said, "Since the temple has been destroyed, upon what shall the Buddha rely for his dwelling? The Master replied, "The Buddhas of antiquity have passed away; now the Buddha returns once more. The King was greatly pleased.
The King asked again, "What is meant by the 'thick gruel of Jiang' spoken of by the monastics? The Master said, "I thought Your Highness had forgotten.
The King asked, "What is meant by the 'three pairs of socks' spoken of by the monastics? The Master replied, "The mountains within the realm."

Having traversed the entire land, this morning he personally arrived at the imperial palace. He was bestowed the title of Chan Master Guanghui Yuanwu, Dharma heir of Chan Master Fu of Mount Jing, and Chan Master Nanchu Yue of Mount Jing in Hangzhou;
he was a native of Longxing. Ascending the hall, he said: "To awaken to the Way upon hearing sound, to see form..."
"Clarifying the Mind. He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "This is form. He struck the ground once and said, "This is sound.
Everyone sees this and hears this; but what is the mind that clarifies? What is the Way that is realized?
He let out a shout and said, "For the sake of a single grain of rice, one loses six months' worth of provisions. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Foci Faxi.
Chan Master Fuzhong Huixin of Tianjie Monastery in Nanjing was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tantan of Tiantong. He was the son of the Jiang family of Fenghua in Ming China.

Having gone to study under Zhuxi, Zhuxi recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma; however, he treated him with a stern countenance and did not exchange a single word with him. The Master’s doubts grew ever more intense. One day—
Ascending the hall to the west, [Wuxie] raised the story of Xinghua striking Kebin and questioned the Master. The Master said, "How magnificent! A lion cub. Wuxie nodded his head in approval.
In the year of Bingyin during the Taiding era, he resided at Guanyin in Mingzhou; later, he resided at Longxiang. When the Ming troops descended upon Jinling, the monks of the temple dispersed.
The Master alone sat in *paryaṅka* (full lotus posture). Soldiers with weapons filled the space before him, but they cast down their staves and prostrated themselves.

The Emperor Gaozu once visited his temple, where the Master expounded the essentials of the Dharma. Praising the Master’s pure and sincere conduct and words, the Emperor specially renamed Longxiang Monastery "Dajianjie.
One day, he wrote a verse: "Throughout my life, I have acted as a mediator for others; for seventy-eight years, I have let things leak out. This morning, I cast off my hands and depart;
ten thousand miles of clear sky, a single flake of snow. On the day before his passing into stillness, he [wrote another].
Just as the Emperor Gao was supervising the army at Jiangyin, he dreamed that the Master came to pay his respects. The Emperor asked, "For what purpose have you come, Master?

The Master replied, "I am about to return westward and have come to bid you farewell. Shortly thereafter, when the imperial carriage returned to Jinling, the Emperor heard the news of the Master's passing;
it coincided exactly with the dream. Struck with wonder and amazement, the Emperor issued an edict to disburse funds from the inner treasury to assist with the funeral arrangements.
Chan Master Qianyan Yuanchang of Mount Fulong in Wuzhou,
the twenty-third generation descendant of Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben of the Southern Peak (Nanyue), was the son of the Dong family of Xiaoshi in Yue. His ancestral lineage...
Zongru studied secular texts from the age of nine; upon merely seeing them, he could recite them by heart. At nineteen, he shaved his head at Lingzhi Temple in Wulin.
During a vegetarian feast for monks hosted by the Chancellor Xing, the Master joined the assembly to receive alms.

It happened that Zhongfeng was seated there, who called out to him, "How do you spend your daily life? The Master replied, "I recite the Buddha's name. Zhongfeng asked, "Where is the Buddha now? The Master—
As he was about to deliberate on this, Feng shouted at him with a stern voice. The Master then knelt and requested the essential points of the Dharma.
Feng bestowed upon him the "Mu" (No) kōan of Zhaozhou and instructed him to investigate it. Thereupon, he bound himself in straw huts among the mountains of Lingyin.

Before long, however, he was moved again due to other duties. Following the conditions of the world, ten years passed in an instant. He returned once more to Lingyin and sat for three years without his side even touching the mat. Because he went there...

At Wangting, he heard the cry of a magpie and attained a realization. He hurried to see Feng and fully explained the cause of his awakening, but Feng again rebuked him. The Master returned home in indignation;
as night was falling into silence, he suddenly noticed a mouse eating a cat’s food that had fallen into its bowl, making a sound. At that moment, he attained a sudden and profound awakening.
He went again to consult with Feng. Feng asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? The Master replied, "The rat ate the cat's food. Feng said, "Not yet.
The Master said, "The vessel for the food has been broken. Feng asked, "What is it like after it is broken? The Master said, "It is reduced to crushed tiles. Feng then smiled.
Later, while presiding over the assembly, he said: "The waters at Longmen are swift; one phrase cuts across the current. The thatched cottage..."
The wind is high; waves rise from a thousand mountains. The Buddhas of the three periods of time hold their tongues in awe;
the patriarchs of the six generations have cause to rub their foreheads in wonder. The old monks throughout the land look up with admiration and admiration.
Now that you all have arrived here, how will you meet this mountain monk? Suddenly he brandishes his staff and says: "In this very way, both man and environment are snatched away."
"Not so, not so; illumination and function are simultaneous. He struck the ground once and said, "A dragon gives birth to a golden phoenix chick, which pierces through the azure lapis lazuli.
A monk asked, "What is it that all the sages of the past have transmitted? The Master said, "Originally there is not a single thing;
its brilliance shakes heaven and earth. The monk asked, "How do you help people? The Master said, "A mouse eating..."
"Cat-food. A monk said, "I do not understand, Master. The Master said, "The bowl falls to the ground, smashing the monastery's bricks.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "To have a mouth like one who is mute.
The monk asked, "What is the second phrase? The Master said, "To have eyes like one who is blind. The monk asked, "What is the third phrase? The Master said, "Even the staff has been broken."
"I have not yet released you. The Master then threw down his whisk and said, "This is the old monk’s second phrase.
What is the first phrase? The Master then descended from his seat. A monk asked, "What is the style of your household, Reverend?

The Master replied, "I lack the strength to raise my fist. Shifa Beishang entered the hall. The spring snow has just cleared, and the spring rain has newly brightened the sky. The flowers are red and the willows are green.

The waters are emerald and the mountains are azure; purple swallows and yellow orioles discourse deeply on the *dharmatā*. The groves of trees and the blades of grass all become the sound of the lute.
It pierces through the nostrils of Śākyamuni and opens wide the eyes of Bodhidharma.
Just as it is today, this single piece of Dharma-cloth offered by Lady Zhang Dezhen of Qijun contains one scroll of the *Heart Sūtra*; it is called "one scroll."
The Heart Sutra is once again a single Dharma-robe; called a single Dharma-robe, it is also a single scroll of the Heart Sutra. Golden flames flicker; brocade layers upon layers.
Interlocking patterns and cross-hatched textures form a multitude of precious seals; extending through the ten directions, clusters of pearl tassels hang in every direction.
The adornments are wondrous, and the marks of virtue increase ever further. Each and every one flows forth from the hearts of the ladies. One...
First, regarding the perfect clarity within the realm of all Buddhas: this old monk has received what none of you possess; you all have received what this old monk does not possess.
It would be better to strike back and return to the monastery’s common property. For a thousand years, ten thousand ages, let the true lamp shine! Let the true lamp shine!
Furthermore, what could he rely upon? At times, hanging it toward the Flower King Throne, it is surely superior to the black-lacquered screens of all other quarters.

On the fourteenth day of the sixth month in the *dingyou* year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested a slight illness. He gathered the assembly and wrote a verse, saying: "Throughout my life I have been loquacious; today my failure is exposed.

One phrase roars through the heavens, and the Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished. Thereupon, he cast down his brush and passed away. His posthumous title was Fohui Yuanjian (Buddha-Wisdom Perfect Mirror).
Chan Master Lintu Weize of the Lion Forest Monastery in Suzhou was the son of the Tan family of Yongxin, Jixian. In his youth, he entered the monastic order at Heshan to receive the tonsure.
Later, he traveled to Tianmu Mountain, where he relied upon Zhongfeng. Whenever he saw Zhongfeng, [Weize] would address him as "Old Huanyou."
While practicing Chan, Sheng failed to attain enlightenment. He harbored private doubts in his heart until he later received the essential instruction and came to master the subtleties of Chan.
Addressing the assembly, a monk asked: "The Buddhas hand it on to one another, and the Patriarchs transmit it from one to the next; ultimately, what is it that they transmit?"
The Master said, "I have already given you thirty blows before your feet even crossed the threshold.

[The monk] asked, "If Bodhidharma had not come to this eastern land and the Second Patriarch had not gone to the Western Heaven, would there still have been a way for him to benefit others? The Master said, "There was.

[The monk] asked, "What is the Master’s way of benefiting others? The Master said, "In the bathhouse, the lanterns laugh until half their mouths are split open. [The monk] said, "Is it not just this?"
"Is this the place where the practitioner turns their body? The Master said, "There is no road to heaven above; there is no door to enter the earth below.
The monk said, "Today I am most fortunate to have heard the lion’s roar. The Master then gave a shout. The monk bowed. The Master said, "As for bowing, you may bow as you please."
This one shout has never been cast down. Then, striking the whisk, he called to the assembly, saying: "Before the sound, there is a path not transmitted by the thousand sages;
it does not depart from its current place, but is ever limpid and still. He let out a shout. "Picked up at random with the hand, it undergoes ten thousand transformations and a thousand changes;
yet when you seek it, you know it cannot be seen. He let out another shout. Now tell me: are these two shouts the same or different?
If you say they are the same, how can it be that there are two shouts? If you say they are different, how can it be that they are but one?
If you understand this point, even a flame will not hinder a mosquito from landing; if you do not understand this point, a lotus fiber will pull the Iron Kunlun Mountain.
If you are a person of stubborn character, do not ask whether they are the same or different, nor whether you have understood or not; simply take what the ancients said...
Two phrases. The two shouts I, this mountain monk, let out are simultaneously cast away beyond the boundaries of other worlds.

Yet look at this homeless man manifesting all manner of divine and demonic forms; sometimes he swallows up the void of the ten directions, leaving all sentient and insentient beings with no way to emerge;
sometimes he releases the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, letting the myriad phenomena be as they are.
The myriad phenomena pervade the entire realm, extending both vertically and horizontally.
At this point, you may not call it "ever-abiding and serene right where one is," nor may you call it "if you seek it, you will know it is invisible.

You may not view them as divided into two parts, nor may you view them as merged into one. It cannot be grasped; it cannot be relinquished. Within this state of unobtainability—*anupalabdhi*—there is only...
“Mòdé! Do you understand? Only through realization can one know that it is difficult to fathom. When the wooden shrine was completed, he addressed the assembly:
“Birth-and-death and nirvana—six times six is thirty-six. Impermanence and the like do not come; I shall first close my eyes. O virtuous practitioners of Zen!
Tell me, is Tianru now dead or alive? If he were dead, he would have brought Tianru back to life; if he were alive, he would have brought Tianru to death.
Buddha after Buddha undergoes saṃsāra solely because of this very thing. He entered parinirvāṇa and was interred at Suixi Yuan.
Zen Master Ingen Gyōyū of Kenchō-ji Zen Temple in Sagami Province, Japan, was originally a native of that province.
His surname was Fujiwara, and he belonged to the nobility of the realm. At the age of thirteen, he shaved his head and traveled extensively through various monasteries, yet he attained nothing.
He subsequently entered China to visit Wu Jian at Huading Peak; there, Wu directed him to visit Zhongfeng. The Master repeatedly presented his insights to Zhongfeng. Zhongfeng—
He rebuked him. The Master’s eating and drinking were both abandoned. Feng, moved by his sincerity, said: "This mind encompasses all phenomena;

in delusion it is birth and death, in awakening it is nirvana. The delusion of birth and death is indeed not easily cast off, and the awakening of nirvana is still like a speck of gold dust entering the eye.
You should know that Prajñā is like a great mass of fire: to draw near to it is to scorch one's head."
With his forehead scorched, he retained only a single thought of non-retrogression: "To live is to live together; to die is to die together. Thus, he naturally accorded with the Way.

Even if, while one has not yet attained awakening, thousands of Śākyamunis and ten thousand Maitreyas were to pour forth, or the great waters of the four seas were to enter one's faculty of hearing—all would be nothing but false and weary toil;
none of it would be the ultimate matter. When the Master heard this, he was deeply moved.
He was so moved that he broke into a cold sweat. One day, having attained a realization, he told Feng, "I have finally managed to crash through the silver mountains and iron walls.
Feng said, "Since you have entered the silver mountains and iron walls, what are you doing here? The Master attained a transcendent understanding.
Later, he took his leave and went to study under various great masters, including Gulin and Dongyu. When Qingzhuo Cheng was about to travel to Japan, he invited the Master to accompany him.
He traveled together [with his master] and subsequently entered the world at Keirin-ji in Koshu. He later moved to various temples, including Manshu-ji, Jōchi-ji, and Chōju-ji.

One day, while slightly ill, he said to his attendant, "The time has come. Bring me a brush and inkstone. He then said, "My stupa is already completed; it is only that the plaque has not yet been inscribed.
He then wrote the two characters *Shin-in* (Mind-Seal) in large script and passed away. Initially, his disciples wished to have a portrait of the Master painted.
As if pre-empting such words of praise, the Master drew a perfect circle and inscribed upon it: "The wondrous marks are perfectly luminous;
as suchness, they are unmoving. Encountering them at every point—what face is this?"
Zen Master Guimei Zhengyou of Gaoyang Mountain in Jianning Prefecture was a successor of Zen Master Chengchan of Shengyan. He was the son of the Ding family of Guixi in Guangxin.
Having left home to become a monk at a young age, he took Master Benshan Ben as his teacher. While traveling through Jianghuai, Jiangnan, and Zhejiang, he visited various spiritual masters. One day—
One day, while urinating and touching the ground, he found an entry point. He requested further instruction from Jue Xue (the details of which are found in the "Chapter on Jue Xue").

Upon reaching Xueyan, he read the *Fachang Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Fachang); when he reached the phrase "driving the plow and seizing the food," he suddenly attained a thorough realization, and sweat broke out involuntarily.
He then composed verses on several *gong'an* cases and sent them to Jue Xue for presentation. Jue Xue said, "This man has received the breath of my bamboo staff for the third time."
He possessed great power, yet he still lacked the shedding of his shell. Three years later, while passing through the hall, he struck a bowl and suddenly attained great enlightenment.

He went forth to reside at T'ien-hsin and subsequently at Kao-ang. Entering the hall for formal discourse, he said: "The sword of wisdom is held aloft alone; the bright command is issued with rectitude.
If you hesitate or deliberate, you shall lose your body and forfeit your life. Is there anyone here who can face this head-on? After a long silence, he said: "Just right—a single sail."
The wind passes over the sea; within this, one does not encounter the one who masters the surging waves. Small Assembly (Xiaocan): When the moon sets behind the mountain peak, it is mournful;
when clouds span the valley mouth, it is dark. If you wish to clarify the matter of birth and death, point directly to the original mind.

Is there anyone here who understands the original mind? When the night is still, there is no need to borrow the moon again; the jade hare always dwells within the great void. The fifth [month] of the Renchen year of the Zhizheng era.
On the third day of the first month, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
His entire body was enshrined within a stone stupa.
Zen Master Zhizhan Dexiang of Hangzhou, a native of Hangzhou and a successor of Zen Master Pingshan Lin, once leaned against his seat and said: "A group of wine-drinkers..."
Fool! What can I do against you? It is not said that he finally entered nirvana.
Chan Master Yizhi of the lineage of Chan Master Dejin Puren of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Zhao family of Lanxi in Wuzhou. At the age of ten, he received the tonsure.

Fahai was thoroughly enlightened; as their karmic conditions were in harmony, he was appointed as his attendant for the incense. In the year of Yiwu during the Zhizheng era, he resided at Xifeng in Jinhua.
When the Great Emperor Taizu took possession of Wuzhou, he visited Zhezhe Chan Temple and issued an imperial decree appointing the Master to reside there.
In the evening, he arrived at Nanping. Suddenly manifesting a slight illness, he counted on his fingers and said, "It is now the fifth month of summer. Those around him replied, "Indeed.
The Master said, "The eighth day of the eighth month is most auspicious; I shall depart then. When morning came, he adjusted his robes, sat upright, and passed away.
Chan Master Lan-yun Zhian of Bian-shan Bai-lan Temple in Huzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Hai-men Ze. He was the son of the Shen family of Jiaxing.

He left home life at Jing-miao Temple in Hai-chang and first visited Tian-zhen, through whom he clarified the essential meaning of the "special transmission outside the teachings. From that time on...
Tao Guang declined invitations from renowned monasteries. In strict accordance with the final instructions of Chan Master Zhuzhang, he resided at Bailian Temple.
He addressed the assembly: "The myriad dharmas return to the One—this is like casting an unperforated iron hammer directly before one’s face.

Where does the One return? It sweeps past both the Western Heaven and this land. The Qingzhou monk’s robe weighs seven catties; on the cold crags and ancient trees, the jade flowers bloom in spring. O worthy ones!"
He inquired with earnest persistence about the ultimate point. "The nostrils born of one's mother have been straight from the beginning.

Had he understood beneath these words, he would have known that the return to nine-nine (eighty-one) clearly reveals eighty-one. Later, he returned to Jingmiao; after a long time, he announced his end on the pretext of illness and was interred in a south-facing field at Cangbian.

Chan Master Baoyun Zhidu of Fulin Monastery in Chuzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Huading Du. He was the son of the Wu family of Lishui in Chu. He received the tonsure from Chan Master Jia Kong.
Having deeply cultivated meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he went to consult Chan Master Wujian, asking: "I do not yet understand the secret intent of the West."
"How is it? Jujian said, "Wait until Mount Salar nods its head, and then I will tell you. As the Master reached out his hand from afar as if to answer, Jujian suddenly shouted.
The Master said, "At the summit of Mount Salar, white waves surge to the heavens; flowers bloom after芒種 (Mangzhong), and leaves fall before立秋 (Liqiu).
Jujian said, "In my house, there are no leftovers of soup or rice. The Master said, "This is not leftover soup."
"What is this leftover rice? he asked. The Master nodded his head in assent. Later, the Ruler [the Emperor] extended universal compassion to all monasteries.

In the *jǐyǒu* year of the Hongwu era, the Master responded to the imperial summons; shortly thereafter, he withdrew to Fulin Monastery. One day, he wrote a verse: "There is no world from which to take leave; there is only the assembly with whom to part.

Within the vast void, why must one drive in a stake? Having cast down his brush, he passed away. Throughout his life, the Master guided others according to their capacities, composing numerous verses and hymns.
It was not permitted for others to record this.
[The following is] a separate lineage of the Dharma heirs of Chan Master Yuan:
Chan Master Mingzhou Tiantong Yuanming Yuanliang, a native of the Zhou family of Ninghai. He first resided at Ruiyan in Tai.
Yan succeeded as the Abbot of Tiantong. His eulogy for Chan Master Hongzhi reads: "Alas! A mountain does not refuse the dust, and thus it can achieve its height;

the ocean does not refuse the flowing streams, and thus it can achieve its depth. Were the Master not one who had previously prepared the wheel of vows for the six perfections and ten thousand practices, how could he have established the merit of this Great Dharma throughout antiquity and the present? When a Sage appears in the world..."

He became a teacher for a hundred generations; once in a thousand years, only the Master attained this. The towering stupa anchors this eastern valley, and the true regulations of the Dongshang school are restored once more.
This humble inscription is deeply engraved upon the cliffs and ravines, praying that the Master may return again to serve as a model for the Dharma.

Chan Master Da’an Puzhuang of Yunju in Fuzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tiantong Yi. He was the son of the Yuan family from Xianju in Taizhou. His mother dreamed that a Buddhist monk entered her chamber before she gave birth to him.
At the age of one, he was precocious and exceptionally gifted. Carrying his book-bag, he entered the local school, where he mastered the texts he was taught through mere recitation.
He relied upon Zha’an of Tiantong for a long time to receive the tonsure. Having received full ordination, he donned the robes at Tianning Monastery in Junzhou and went to attend upon Liaotang.
The Master asked, "Where have you come from? The teacher replied, "Tiantong. The Master said, "Changyu, braving the cold, what such urgent death-pressing business do you have?

The teacher replied, "Precisely because the matter of birth and death is urgent. The Master asked, "What is this urgent matter of birth and death? The teacher made a striking gesture with his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*).
The Abbot said, "Dare you come here to pull a tiger’s whiskers? Go to the Hall! One day, while in the hall, the Abbot raised the koan of the cypress tree in the courtyard.
As the Master was about to open his mouth, the Abbot struck him across the face with his palm. He attained sudden enlightenment.

In the *Jihwei* year of the Hongwu era, the Master took up residence at Beichen Monastery in Fuzhou. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Yesterday I cleared the wasteland; I ask all of you to weed it out."
The thorns and brambles have been cleared away, and the original foundation is now clearly visible. Only the tree in the center remains, and no one has been able to uproot it.
Today, this mountain monk cannot help but employ another expedient means: with a sharp blade, I shall prune away all the profuse branches and leaves;
with a blunt hoe, I shall deeply dig out the crooked and inverted roots. When the work upon the solid ground is completed as a single whole, the axe for dwelling in the mountains will be finished.
Wumeng. Whenever the Master saw a monk, he would ask: "Recently, we have received official documents ordering that you must be thoroughly investigated, Venerable One.
The monk would say, "I am not a spy. The Master would say, "Even so, you must be interrogated before you can go. The monk would say, "Master, do not abuse your power to oppress others.
The Master would extend his hand and say, "Bring me your warrant! As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him with his palm. This was "Clearing the Weeds."
Next, a monk asked, "When will this patch of ground be cleared until it is clean? The Master raised his hoe and said, "It must not be called a hoe.
I wonder, Elder, what would you call it? The monk was speechless. The Master threw down the hoe and said, "When will this patch of ground be cleared until it is clean?
Question: "Riding on the tiger’s head, lashing the tiger’s tail—what is the middle?"
"What about this intervening matter? The Master said, "He has attained freedom. The monk asked, "As for what the ancients said, 'I too cannot bring it forth'—what is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Entering the water, one sees the tall man. The monk requested further instruction.
The Master said, "What is lacking within your own self that you come to request instruction? As the monk was about to respond, the Master said, "You only know how to covet..."
Cheng Bu did not notice he had lost his way. He asked, "What is the realm of Yunju? The Master said, "The road turns, the stream bends, and the empty courtyard is still.

Cheng asked, "Who is the person within the realm? The Master said, "In an era of great peace, one’s body is free. Cheng said, "I have already received your instruction regarding the person and the realm;
I wish to hear a single phrase for a beginner. The Master said, "A featherless hawk flies close to the sky."

Fei asked, "When one encounters a person who has attained the Way on the road, and they do not respond with either speech or silence, what then? The Master said, "Only one who has attained the Way knows.
Fei said, "How can you, Master, meet me with such a clash of swords? The Master said, "It is better to frighten a thief than to catch him.
Fei said, "A man of clear eyes cannot be deceived for even a single point. The Master said, "I knew at once that you did not have good intentions. [Up] (The next case begins here)
The Hall. When I, this old monk, was clearing the wasteland, I dug up a blunt axe from the foundation of the Dharma Hall. I have kept it for a long time among my brothers;
if there is anyone who can make use of it, I shall entrust it to them with both hands. If you cannot carry its weight, I shall keep it myself. Why such a desperate hurry?
It would be better to cast it away at the head of the refuse heap, letting it be scorched by the sun and battered by the wind.
[He] blew [the dust] away. Suddenly picking up his staff, he struck it once and said: "Whipping up the iron ox to plow the great earth—who could plant crabapples at the bottom of a well?
In the spring of the twenty-sixth year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued summoning eminent monks from throughout the realm;

the Master was selected as the foremost. His responses before the Emperor met with imperial approval. In the autumn, he received an imperial decree to offer sacrifices at Mount Lu. When the rites were completed, he returned.
He was granted an imperial gift of a full set of robes. That winter, he received the decree to ascend and reside at Mount Jing. Entering the hall, he said:
"Since the beginning of birth and Buddhahood, those who have preached the Dharma like clouds and rain are beyond counting.

Today at Mount Jing, we shall temporarily borrow empty space as a mouth and Mount Sumeru as a tongue to proclaim the Dharma-gate of the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
Sentient and insentient beings all at once, with different mouths but one voice, praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Rare, rare indeed!
Is there anyone among the assembly who does not find this agreeable? Come forth and meet this staff! [The Master] took up the staff, struck it once, and said:
"Contemplate closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. [He] ascended the hall. From Mount Lu...
Come! I have received a letter from Huading, reporting that the white-fanged tiger of Nanshan is actually hiding its fangs and crouching its claws within the Dragon Abyss.
As for the crimson-scaled carp of the Eastern Sea, it has leaped straight up to the peak of Vulture Mountain, surging through the waves—excellent!
Great assembly, where in the entire Great Canon of the Teachings has such a thing ever been spoken? Nevertheless, the staff of Jingshan is not yet willing to let it pass.
Standing there, he took up his staff, drew a line in the air, and said, "The immortal Zhang Guolao does not care for his medicinal gourd.
Leaning on his staff, he descended from the seat. Suddenly, on the twenty-third day of the tenth month, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Difficult, difficult!
A beautiful young maiden of sixteen climbs a high mountain; even this old monk cannot support her. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Chan Master Jianxin Laifu of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yue of Mount Jing. He was the son of the Wang family of Fengcheng in Nanchang.

He received the tonsure at Xifang Temple in his native district and vowed to eliminate all external conditions in order to directly clarify the wondrous purport of *nirvāṇa*. After a long time, his entire being became [unobstructed].
Ai visited Nanchu. Nanchu took a liking to him and retained him as the Director of Internal Records.

Initially, he resided at Dingshui in Yue, where he built a cottage by an eastern stream and named it "Reed Hermitage" (*Pó-ān*) to express his filial devotion to his mother, the Lady of Muzhou. He closed the gate and addressed the assembly: "My body is like withered wood, a hundred thoughts have turned to ash.
The mountain monkeys and wild cranes suspect me with distress. I close my door alone amidst the rain upon the green pines; When meeting a smile, I encounter [the Way]."

People were also too lazy to open [the text]. He once composed a verse on the White Ox, saying: Plowing clouds, he never stops at the eastern gate of the sea; He gathers them toward the small peak of Laṅkā.
On the open ground, he has already forgotten the power of taming; Who on the Snowy Mountains can recognize his coming and going? Released back to the Jeta Grove, he follows the sheep and deer;

Having cultivated the *tathāgata-puṣpa*, he accompanies the elephants and dragons. In the uniformity of the sky’s end, his horns and head are distinct; Water... (Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)

A jade lotus in a pool of refined essence. In the winter of the first year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned for his lofty conduct to preach the Dharma at Mount Zhong and was granted a meal in the inner court.
At that time, Prince Zhu Chang of Shu was held in special affection by the Taizu;
he commanded the Confucian scholars Li Shijing and Su Bohe to discourse on the Way with the Master and others every day without fail. Prince Zhu of Shu treated the Master with great—

In the year Gengwu (1590), he was ordered to compose four admonitions—*Zuoxin* (Sitting in Mindfulness), *Guandao* (Observing the Way), *Chongben* (Honoring the Root), and *Jingxian* (Reverencing the Worthy)—which were posted in the palace for his own edification.

In the twentieth year, at the age of twenty, he was arrested by the Shanxi authorities as a member of the Hu faction; because he had been in frequent contact with the Hu residence, he was charged with a crime and executed.

Chan Master Wuzhi Ke of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Ming of Lingyin. He was the son of the Li family from Linhai in Taizhou. At the age of nineteen, he received full ordination.

He sighed, saying: "That which is most precious for one who is a bhikṣu is the diligent pursuit of investigating and clarifying the essence of the mind. If one is merely entangled in and obscured by literary texts..."
While contemplating the characteristics of written characters, he wondered when he might be able to attain liberation. Taking up his staff, he departed to visit Pujue.
During their exchange of questions and answers, his doubts were suddenly resolved, and Pujue approved of him. In the sixth year of the Zhiyuan era, he resided at Mount Daxiong in Taizhou;

later, he lived at Jingci Monastery. When his end approached, the assembly requested a verse. The Master said, "In our school, there is fundamentally no speech," and with palms joined, he passed away in stillness.
Chan Master Wanfeng Shiwei of Mount Dengwei in Suzhou,
the twenty-fourth generation descendant of the Linji lineage under Chan Master Fulong Chang and a native of the Jin family of Leqing, Wenzhou, went to visit Master Zhi.
Yan instructed him with the "Three Not-Sos" (san bushi) and he departed for the ruins of the ancient Foji Temple on Mount Dapeng, where he built a hermitage.
One day, upon hearing the temple master cite the koan of Muzhou kicking over the water pitcher, he suddenly attained enlightenment. He immediately spoke this verse:

"Toppling and overturning" was Nanquan; it exhausted my efforts for half a year. Had you been able to personally realize it at that very moment, how could he have failed to deliver a fist-blow straight to your chest?
Wufeng went to visit Wuji. Wuji asked, "All dharmas return to One; where does the One return?
The Master stepped forward, paid his respects, and stood with his hands joined in *añjali*. Wuji asked, "What is the Way? The Master replied, "The Way has no..."
[Zhaozhou] said, "It can be spoken. Jian said, "If it can be spoken, it is 'not the Way. What is it that is not the Way? The Master said, "I am precisely wanting the Master to have doubts.
Jian said, "To have doubts is an error. The Master said, "Not to have doubts is also an error. Jian gave a shout. The Master also shouted. Jian shouted again.
The Master also shouted and shook out his sleeves, departing. He went to study under Qianyan. Qianyan asked, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha..."
"What is this thing? The Master took up his sitting cloth, drew a circle, and stood with his hands folded.
Xueyan said, "With what will you meet this old monk? The Master raised his fist and said, "I meet the Master here.
Xueyan said, "When one dies and is cremated, where does one establish one's body and life? The Master said, "The bubble arises; the bubble perishes."
The water remained; the wind had ceased and the waves were calm as the moon reflected upon the pool. Yankuan asked, "Do you wish to request further instruction and receive the precepts?

The Master covered his ears and departed. The next day, Yankuan invited the assembly to cut pine trees. The Master picked up a round stone, made the gesture of offering a pearl, and said, "I ask the Master to set its price.
Yankuan said, "It is not worth half a coin. The Master said, "Blind! Yankuan said, "I am blind too."
"You are also blind," the Master said. "Blind, blind! He then spoke this verse: "The daughter of the Dragon Palace offered a pearl, Its value was three thousand times that of the great trichiliocosm.
Yet it was seen through by a bystander; Who would have known it was not worth half a penny? One day, as Yanguan ascended the seat, he cited the saying:
"The windless lotus leaf moves; there must surely be a fish swimming beneath. The Master stepped forth from the assembly and roared with a thunderous voice.
With a single shout, he shook out his sleeves and departed. Yunyan presented a verse, saying: "Thick yellow chrysanthemums fill the eyes;
autumn is here. Baizhang sits upright atop the green peak. Lightly bringing forth the phrase 'no guest and no host,' A single shout makes the waters of a thousand rivers flow backward.
The Master then went to Mount Song in Lanxi Prefecture to build a hermitage. Entering the hall, he extended both hands and said: "I open wide the gate of expedient means. Then—
Entering from within this [space], he again clenched his two fists and said, "The secure gate is closed; let us speak of matters from within the house.
He then asked, "Tell me, how would you express that which is neither opened nor closed? After a long silence, he gathered up his *saṃghāṭī* robe and descended from the seat.
Later, he moved his staff to Dengwu and established a great monastery named Sheng'en. On the twentieth day of the first month in the fourteenth year of the Hongwu era...

On the ninth day, he sat in meditation and spoke this verse: "For seventy-nine years, I have tasted only the flavor of the weeded field; with hands released from the precipice, the bright sun shines in the sky.
Having finished speaking, he passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the western ridge of the mountain.
Chan Master Weian Deran of Songyin in Songjiang Prefecture was the son of the Zhang family of that district. In his youth, he shaved his head under Master Guyong Wuyong;

subsequently, he visited Qianyan, and upon hearing his formal teachings, he attained sudden and thorough enlightenment. Later, he succeeded him as the abbot of that seat. One day, ascending the hall, he said:
"The New Year begins its reign, and all things flourish. He then suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Yesterday, this staff..."
Last night it sent forth shoots; this morning it has shed its buds. The flower opens five petals, and its fragrance pervades the great trichiliocosm.
Tell me, is there any Buddha-dharma to be found at the head of the New Year? [He plants his staff and lets out a shout. Entering the hall: Heaven has no gate; earth has no door.
A swift and capable monk may come and go as he pleases. The *maṇi* jewel within the treasury illuminates the ten directions;
the peach blossoms in the cavern compete to bloom in a thousand petals. Borrowing the spring breeze from beyond kalpas, it accords with the pitch-pipes of the present age.

At midnight, the Sea God gazes upon the shark’s pearl; the light of his eyes hangs suspended from the tree of Fǔsāng. (He gives a shout. Entering the hall: the wax man serves as the verification. At last—

Today, at the conclusion of the ninety-day retreat, as merits are evaluated and the ultimate truth discerned, the Yellow-Faced Old Gautama has tied up the mouth of his sack, causing hundreds of thousands of devas and humans to all suffer indignity.
At Songyin, however, the retreat is not conducted in such a manner. Making a gesture with his hands as if rowing a boat, he said:
"I, this mountain monk, am now launching an iron boat without a bottom; I invite the entire assembly to enter the Great [Dharma] together."
"The Perfect Enlightenment Ocean goes out to play! He gave a shout and said, "Look at the precious rope atop the stupa on the fixed compass.
He ascended the hall and said: "The hook and the rope are linked; the link and the hook are the rope. Fully manifesting in their very essence, eye meets eye.
Horizontally, they pierce through the nose-tip of empty space; vertically, they lock the iron pillar of Mount Sumeru. Personally from evil..."
This was forged through the intense heat of the fiery tongs; how can it be compared to the ordinary practice of wrapping it in paper and binding it with hemp?

Layman Gubaogao’s grand vision of the stupa is a work that soars through the present and spans the ages. Nevertheless, tell me: how shall one express this single phrase of being "highly suspended and hanging upside down"?
With the four eaves level and settled, fragrant clouds swirl about; its brilliance shall illuminate ten thousand generations. The Buddha.
On the day of the long calendar, Chan Master Wuyong Shougui of Tiantong Monastery in Hangzhou was born into the Zhang family of Pujiang, Wuzhou.

Having first studied under Qianyan and attained a sudden realization, he subsequently visited Zhongfeng and other venerable masters, who remarked: "Though a thousand rivers differ, the bright moon is one."
"It is one and the same. From now on, I have no further doubts. In the year Gengyin of the Zhizheng era, while presiding over Tiantong Monastery, he wrote a verse on the day of his passing:
"This single stinking shell of a snail—inside and out, foul and vile—I cast it aside and go forth. Shaking the bell in space, Tiantong’s single finger:
today is just like yesterday. Having cast down his brush, he passed away.
The verse of farewell by Master Chang’an Mingsou of Huashan in Jinhua Prefecture, when he took leave of the assembly, says: "Birth is fundamentally not birth;
extinction likewise has no extinction. Casting off the hand, one simply goes—like a sliver of moon in the void. He then sat upright and passed away.
Chan Master Konggu Longjing of Zhengzhuan Monastery in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Bailian An. He was the son of the Chen family from Mount Dongting in Suzhou.
While still a child, he abstained from meat and sat in meditation as if in *dhyāna*. He received his monastic precepts from Bian Shan Lanyun and studied Chan; although he remained at home...
While residing there, he visited and paid his respects to all the eminent Chan masters of the "lake and sea" tradition, such as Guzhu and others.

Later, he took Shi’an of Huqiu as his teacher. In the second year of the Xuande era, he received full ordination at Zhaqing Temple in Hangzhou. He subsequently followed Shi’an to reside at Lingyin Monastery.

In the seventh year, he traveled to Mount Tianmu to pay homage at the ancestral pagoda. He stayed there for one year, engaging in rigorous and diligent investigation until he suddenly attained realization. Thereupon, he proceeded to...

Laiyun exposed the truth, and Yunyin certified his realization. The Master showed this to Jingtang, saying: "That which is the 'one step beyond' is like a knotted web-pattern after one has attained thorough enlightenment;
it is a decisive blow, what is called the 'final phrase. It cannot be reached through words or speech;
one must simply employ the skillful means of the living pivot to bring about transformation, as when Baizhang went for a second interview with Mazu. Mazu—
He employed this very device when Linji went for a second visit to Huangbo; Huangbo likewise employed this device. Linji’s striking Luopo was also this device.
It was only later, beneath Jia Shan’s staff, that he finally attained a glimpse of awakening. Xinghua’s striking Kebin was also this device.
Master Zhenjing composed a verse on it, saying: "A man of spirit should sever [doubts] himself; Xinghua did so for him."
This person is a thoroughgoing Han. In time, his own eyes will open for himself. He was bound, fined, and driven out of the monastery;
this verse is most appropriate for such an occasion. You have not yet clarified this public case (kung-an); how can you clarify this one point?

For those who possess spiritual roots from past lives, even a public case is very easy to clarify. Have you not seen that whenever Linji asked about the Buddha-dharma, Huangbo would immediately [strike him]?
"Striking! It is most appropriate. Later, he received a single phrase from Dayu that resolved his doubts, and he thoroughly mastered Huangbo’s pedagogical methods.
Suppose today you were to ask me for the ultimate point; I too would not need to move my lips or stir my tongue—I would simply strike you.
Ask again and I shall strike again. You have been struck by me until you are bewildered, leaving you with no stratagem and no recourse.
It can be said that it is possible; yet whether one might suddenly attain a profound realization within the mind remains unknown.
Although I do not employ blows or shouts, you should simply accept it as such and look into it.

In the ninth year of the Zhengtong era, when the Master was fifty-two years old, he composed his own epitaph for his stupa at Xuji Mountain on West Lake in Wulin. (According to the *Chandeng Shipu*, Konggu Long succeeded Tianru Ze; however, upon reading the *Konggu Ji*...)

It was known that Master [Zhu] was the dharma successor of Lanyun. His own epitaph for the stupa states: "Venerable Lanyun was the preceptor of my preceptor, Jinglong. He attained the orthodox lineage of Linji for twenty generations.

When the Master traces his roots upward to the Heavenly Truth (Tianzhen), there is no fixed rule regarding whether the source is infinite or whether one follows Xueyan Qin; nor is there a fixed order for succession. Succession from the predecessor to the successor is like Ānanda succeeding Kāśyapa;

succession from the successor to the predecessor is like Xinghua succeeding Linji. The principle penetrates past and present, and arriving at the ultimate reality is the supreme goal. Master Zhu feared that those who compiled the *Xu deng lu* (Continued Lamp Record) might cling to this [view] while disparaging others, leading to disputes similar to those between the Tianwang and Tiantai lineages. Therefore, he specifically set this forth.
The Dharma successor of Chan Master Fulin Du was Chan Master Guzhu Jun of Mount Bafeng in Fanchang County, Taiping Prefecture. When Wuji went to visit him, the Master asked, "Return [to me]..."
Ji said, "If there is a function of illumination, it immediately becomes an obstruction. The Master said, "This fellow clings to emptiness; even the Buddha could not save him.
Ji said, "Both existence and non-existence are utterly extinguished; both emptiness and the Buddha are entirely non-existent.
Later, he was shown a verse which said: "I recall the time we parted at Fan-chang; how many people can truly know this mind? The zither-less melody is truly..."
Able to continue [the lineage]. With the life of wisdom hanging in the balance, to whom shall it be entrusted?
The Dharma successor of Chan Master Wei of Dengwei, the twenty-fifth generation under Nanyue.
Xu Bai visited Chan Master Baozang Puchi of Mount Dengwu in Suzhou. The Master asked, "The mind is not the Buddha;
wisdom is not the Way. How do you understand this? Xu Bai stepped forward to inquire after him and stood with his hands clasped.
The Master rebuked him, saying, "After all this time, are you still harboring such views? Xu Bai then became so resolute that he forgot to eat. Upon reaching the second [stage]...
At night, there was a great realization. The Master smiled and said, "Even though it is so, you must still protect and maintain yourself well.
When the time arrives, this principle will manifest itself."
Xu Bai of Guolinsi Chan Temple on Mount Dengwu in Suzhou went to visit the Master. The Master cast down his meditation cushion and demanded a verse.
Xu Bai said, "This very message is fundamentally beyond words; upon this broken meditation cushion, the earth bursts and the heavens split.
The Master asked, "Tell me, what is it that splits? As Xu Bai was about to step forward, the Master struck him.
Chan Master Wunian Shengxue of Jiufeng, Wuchang Prefecture, was a native of Yingzhou, Suizhou. His surname was Chen.

At the age of nine, he took refuge with Master Yuan of Baolin Temple in his home prefecture and left the household life. Initially, he could not read a single character; nevertheless, he applied himself to ascetic practice for many years.

Realizing that his own fundamental matter remained unclarified, he studied under Master Wumen regarding the koan "The myriad dharmas return to one. Subsequently, he entered Mount Song and resided there.

Jing had an awakening one day and composed a verse, saying: "For years at Mount Dong, the mist hung thick; I leaned on the railing all day, waiting for the clear sky. Last night, suddenly the moon rose in the frosty heavens;

Wanfeng presented him with the "Ox Passing Through the Window" koan and commanded him to compose a verse. The Master said: "The horns and head protrude sharply..."
Yong said: "Hooves and hoofs pass through the body as the moon sinks in the west. If you can turn your body at the opportune moment, let out a roar and have no further doubt.
Feng then offered a verse to certify this, after which he returned to Baolin. His reputation for the Way became widely renowned.
King Zhao of Chu built a monastery to invite the Master to reside there. Addressing the assembly, the Master asked: "What is the direct pointing of Bodhidharma?"
A single phrase. The assembly was speechless. The Master spoke on their behalf, saying: "Before the Five Milk Peaks, we discuss the Shaoshi [Mount Sheshan] tradition.
During the Hongwu era, the Taizu summoned him to the Fengtian Hall and personally questioned him on the essentials of the Dharma. The Master presented a verse, which greatly pleased the Emperor;
the Emperor composed a poem and prose to bestow upon him. On the twenty-ninth day of the third month in the third year of the Yongle era (the Yiyou year), he spoke this verse:

He passed away with solemn dignity; his entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Simsan Rock. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Cheongbok Gwanghui (Pure Blessing and Broad Wisdom).

Chan Master Wujie of Donglin in Puzhou, a successor of Chan Master Fan Changjun, was a native of Shu. At the age of twenty, he emerged from worldly entanglements and constructed a hermitage by binding bamboo together.
He applied himself with unremitting diligence, refusing even to look at calligraphic scrolls as large as four fingers. He simply practiced his "dull" work with blind persistence. Later—
He attained great penetration and great awakening. The Master had a verse that said: "Non-thought is attachment to emptiness; thought is attachment to grasping.

its radiance penetrates everywhere. Originally there is neither black nor white; where is there anything that is not encompassed? Chushan came to consult the Master, who asked him about his stay over the past few years.

Dongsan replied, “Originally there was nothing lost; what is there to attain? The Master asked, “Is it not something acquired through study?
Dongsan replied, “Since not a single dharma exists, from where could study come? The Master asked, “Have you fallen into emptiness? Dongsan replied, “I am not even that.”
"I am who? Who has fallen? Who is empty? The Master asked, "Ultimately, what is it like? Shanshan said, "The water is shallow and the stones appear;
the rain has cleared and the clouds have vanished. The Master said, "Do not speak in such a confused manner. Even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to come, they would not be permitted.

Even if you were to swallow the Tripitaka whole and manifest hundreds of thousands of supernatural powers, here you still would not be permitted. Shanshan said, "Although the Master holds the line firm..."
"This is a vital ford; alas, it requires such toil that it is not easy. The Master struck his knee once and asked, "Do you understand? Sanshan gave a shout.
The Master smiled and said, "One who can sustain the family must be one who can break the family. To manage the household affairs in this way is indeed effortless.
Sanshan covered his ears and departed. The Master bestowed upon him a Dharma verse, saying: "I have no Dharma to transmit; you have no mind to receive. With neither transmitting nor receiving mind—"
Who would not achieve success?
Regarding the question asked by the monk from Yangzhou, the Dharma heir of the layman Mimi-an, concerning the path to Putuo: "Through which gate does it exit? The Master said: "Right here."
"From what gate do you enter now? [The monk] said, "Why do you suppress and constrain me? The Master said, "Look under your feet. The monk raised his head and took three steps forward;
the Master said, "Wrong. The monk then retreated three steps; the Master said, "Wrong. The monk was at a loss. The Master said, "Is it your fault, or is it my fault?
[The monk] said, "I already knew it was wrong before you even spoke. The Master pointed to his knee and said, "Right."
"Excellent! Eat! The monk was speechless. The Master said, "When you travel to other places, remember this clearly.
[This concludes the record of] Chan Master Chichi of Dengwu, the twenty-sixth generation descendant under Nanyue. His Dharma heirs:
Chan Master Dongming Xubai Huiyan of Hangzhou was surnamed Wang and was a native of Huguang.
At the age of fourteen, he received the tonsure under Zhanran at Miaojue Temple in Danyang. One day, while engaged in manual labor, Zhanran asked him, "What are you doing here?
The Master replied, "I am slicing radishes. Zhanran said, "You only know how to slice radishes. The Master replied, "That is so."
Huìshān was capable of killing men; yet he presented his neck to his master, who said, "I do not execute those who have surrendered.

When Huìrán resided at Shūshān, he heard that Sōngyǐn was propagating the Way in Yúnjiān, so he went there to seek instruction. One day, emerging from meditative concentration, he looked up at a pine tree and attained realization.
He soon traveled to Dengwu on Mount Su and met Foguo Lin, with whom he felt an immediate affinity like a needle meeting its eye. Lin further pointed him toward Baozang.

The Master recounted the causes of his awakening in detail, but Baozang rebuked him. Thereupon, the Master became so resolute that he forgot both sleep and food. On the second night, he suddenly reached the very bottom of the source of the Dharma.
He spoke in verse: "A single punch shatters the vast void; The billions of Sumeru mountains leave no trace. I borrow..."
Question: "Who is the master within this? Answer: "A single red orb surges forth from the Eastern Sea. In the Wuzi year of the Yongle era, he arrived at Anxi and established a monastery.
For over thirty years, his shadow did not leave the mountain. His reputation spread among both the clergy and the laity, and veteran monks vied with one another to seek instruction at his seat.
From within the hall, he uttered a vertical saying: "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way; the Tripitaka is not the Dharma. What is it?
None of those who offered responses were in accord. He then bestowed the Dharma upon Haizhou and ascended the seat, saying:
"Gautama had an intention for whom to transmit; Kāśyapa opened a smile for no reason. Reaching this point, how could even the Seven Buddhas have any seniority? Even Mañjuśrī’s face turns red."
Stupefied. Today, the matter of Dongming is laughable; it causes people for a thousand ages to waste their spittle.

Fortunately, Master Haengong forgot both self and me, so that the single thread of the Jeong-seon (Jō) lineage continues unceasingly. He threw down his staff and said, "The burden of a thousand catties is now fully entrusted to you.
The profound and the essential are discussed today by this staff. He struck three times with his whisk and descended from the seat. Xuande Xinyou.

On the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month in the year of You, he expressed his intention to pass away. When the assembly requested that he leave behind a verse, the Master said, "The entire Tripitaka of the teachings has no one capable of scrutinizing it;
how could I produce these few idle words? At the hour of Chen on the twenty-ninth day, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
He was interred in a stupa at Dongwu in Anxi.
Chan Master Da-chan of Xuegu in the assembly at Tianjie Mountain in Jianning Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Shouchang Lai, went for an audience. The Master presented him with this verse:

"When myriad conditions all arise together, Let them go and do not be startled by the cold. Simply take the dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges And gather them back into a single mass. [He then] tossed [the whisk].
He overturned all obstacles and shattered the gates of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). He fought back and defeated the ranks of the Māra army; weapons and banners were laid aside in idleness.
When he manifested his realization, the Master praised him, saying: "Truly this golden-haired lion has emerged from its den; the Wheel of Dharma has already been turned and entered the marketplace.
With one roar, 'zhu-di,' it echoes through the vast sky; when wild beasts hear it, their brains split open. He then instructed him with a verse, which began: "Transforming the myriad..."
Perfect penetration: penetrating through all ten directions, there stands alone a True Person. Unfurling the broad and long tongue, the lion’s roar resounds;
the jackals’ heads all burst asunder. Transmitting the lamp from generation to generation, its light remains undimmed to this very day.
Chan Master Chushan Shaoshi of Dongshan Tiansheng Temple in Chengdu Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Wuzu of Donglin. He was the son of the Lei family of Tang’an.
At the age of eight, he entered the local school and mastered the recitation of the classics. At nine, he lost his father and went to Chan Master Xuanji Tong to study the Way.

This was a worldly matter. Later, he went to visit Wuji, who showed him the "Mu" (No) kōan. By chance, he heard the board signaling the end of meditation, and the obstruction in his chest melted away like ice.
He went to see Wuji, who said, "Give me back the meaning of 'Mu'. The Master replied: "That monk’s question was already too much;
how could Old Zhao ever have indulged in thought? A single word spoken offhand has been fully revealed, yet it turns out to be quite superfluous."
Master Ji made him doubt, asking, "What is that place where you have no doubt? The Master replied, "Green mountains and blue waters; swallows warbling and orioles singing;
everything is vividly clear—what more is there to doubt? Ji said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "The head touches the void, while the feet tread upon solid ground.
Ji said, "Still not yet. The Master then prostrated himself. Ji said, "So it is, so it is. Afterward...
He resided at Tianzhu. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Tianzhu? The Master said, "The ravines are wide and clouds return late;
the mountains are high and the sun rises slow. The monk asked, "Who is the person within this realm? The Master said, "Below the forehead, the eyebrows cover the eyes;
on the cheeks, the ears tower over the shoulders. The monk asked, "What is the house style of Tianzhu? The Master said, "A cloud-bowl steams pine powder; an ice-cauldron boils [bamboo shoots]."
Yuet-tuan asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The Sea God has cast forth a night-bright pearl.
Yuet-tuan said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Mañjuśrī has lost his crystal cup. Yuet-tuan asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A cast-iron weight.
Yuet-tuan asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said, "A stone and a clod of earth. Yuet-tuan asked, "What is... [The text ends here.]
A monk asked, "Master, [what is this? The Master said, "A black-lacquered staff. The monk asked, "Who is it that does not encounter cold or heat?
The Master said, "I have already told you; do you recognize him or not? As the monk prepared to respond, the Master rebuked him, saying, "To conceive a thought is to deviate;
to open your mouth is to err. By the time you blink your eyes, the error has already passed. The monk said, "So it is so close, after all! The Master said, "You..."

"What principle have you seen? The monk replied, "The face and features are distinct; they are not revealed when the opportunity arises. The Master let out a thunderous shout, and the monk was suddenly enlightened.
In the fifth year of the Jingtai era, he resided at Touzi. A monk asked, "Having departed from Mount Wan, you now occupy Touzi.
As the assembly gathers before you, we request that you offer prayers for the Emperor. The Master said, "The long-life talisman within the cauldron; on the peak, it does not..."
Lao Song said, "I have already received your instructions regarding the rite for the Emperor; what is the 'house style' of Touzi like?
The Master said, "Carrying a water jar through the marketplace, he is not the oil-seller. Lao Song asked, "As for the Patriarch’s saying, 'Do not travel at night;
you must arrive by dawn,' is this truly so? The Master said, "Though there is sinew in his eyes, alas, he cannot compete with the tongue."
Wugu said, "Zhaozhou said, 'I have already waited for the white; I shall wait further for the black. What is the meaning of this?

The Master said, "If not for the exhaustion of the bow and arrow, he would not yet consent to raise the flag of surrender. A questioner asked, "Today the Master ascended the seat to preach the Dharma.
I wonder what auspicious signs there were? The Master said, "The qilin strides beyond the vermilion heavens; the *utpala* flower blooms amidst the raging fire."
[In the] middle [of the assembly], someone asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The snow melts and the mountain peak is revealed;
the wind passes and the tree tops sway. Ascending the hall, the Master looked over the great assembly and said, "This very thing is a source of confusion for how many monks throughout the ages!
Arriving here, they cannot open their mouths; they cannot fathom it through thought; they cannot bring it forth to be proclaimed. Suddenly, he picked up [a whisk].
Holding up his staff, he said, "For what reason has it today fallen into the hands of this mountain monk? Holding the staff crosswise, he said, "To hold it crosswise is also up to me.
Picking up the staff, he said, "To hold it upright is also up to me. Setting the staff down, he said, "To set it down is also up to me.
Thus, whether rolling it up or spreading it out, killing or giving life—all is entirely up to me. Then, he pointed the staff toward the air.

He struck once and said: "At this very moment, from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old down to the elder monks throughout the land, upon reaching this point, they have no choice but to beg for their lives. Is there anyone among you who can speak out on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
After a long silence, he struck his staff once and said: "I pierce the blind adamantine eye; I topple the precious throne of the Empty King. You..."
"What kind of bowl are you all looking for? one day the Master asked. One day, while visiting a vegetable garden, the Master saw the gardener tying up a gourd vine.
Pointing to a gourd, the Master said, "This one has no mouth; why does it grow so large?
The gardener replied, "I have never been idle for a single moment. The Master said, "Does your master exert some effort on your behalf as well?"
[The monk] said, "There is none; it relies entirely upon other-power. The Master said, "Bring him here to meet this old monk. The monk prostrated.
The Master said, "He is still nothing but a servant or a slave. The monk picked up a bamboo splint used for tying a winter melon trellis. The Master laughed heartily.
Looking back at his attendant, he said, "There are insects in the vegetable garden. On the fifteenth day of the third month in the ninth year of the Chenghua era, he manifested a slight illness.
The assembly requested the Master’s final word. The Master extended both hands and showed them to them, asking, "Do you understand?
They replied, "We do not understand. He spoke again: "On this very day this year, the cart is pushed and hung upon the wall; the void is struck down; a thunderclap in the blue sky. A-he-he!"
The clay ox swallows the old dragon’s pearl; in the limpid ocean of nature, the foam-flowers subside. He then passed away peacefully.
Zen Master Guangshan Baoyuetan of Bafeng Mountain in Taiping Prefecture was visited by Dahui.
The Master asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Dahui replied, "There are clouds upon the eastern ridge. The Master said, "Are there rain-clouds or no rain-clouds?"

Yun said, "The rain pours down in torrents. The Master asked, "What is it like after it has fallen? Yun said, "White waves surge to the heavens. The Master asked, "What is 'the myriad dharmas returning to the One'?
Yun said, "The cold and heat of the human world cannot invade it. The Master asked, "What is the 'Cheongju (Qingzhou) cotton robe'?
Yun said, "Fortunately, it encountered the hand of a skilled craftsman. The Master said, "The bright sun is high in the sky; there is no [darkness]."
"What is it that is not illuminated? Why is it obscured by a fragment of cloud? Huì said, "The boat goes and the boat comes, but the shore does not move.
The Master said, "Every person has a shadow; why is it that one cannot step upon it? Huì said, "Yesterday someone came from Guangdong.
The Master said, "The entire great earth is a pit of fire; what samādhi do you possess such that you are not burned up? Huì [remained silent].
[The master] said, "The carp of the Eastern Sea swallows the sun. The teacher said, "So it is, so it is. He then bestowed upon him a verse, saying:

"Though heaven and earth are vast, they cannot conceal it; Though the sun and moon are bright, they cannot surpass its light. The lamp of wisdom shall be perpetuated and never extinguished, Flowing through the ages and continuing throughout all quarters."
The Dharma-transmission verse of Chan Master Cheng of Taigang and Yuexi in Nanjing says: "The mind is that which can know the mind;
Dharmas are that which can know dharmas. The Dharma-mind now transmitted is neither mind Nor is it dharma."
Chan Master Yuanxin of Wuwai on Mount Funiu was the son of the Gao family of Jintai. He relied upon Master Wuji for investigation and study, later attaining liberation.
His verse says: "The Kunlun Mountains are overturned as the clear wind dances; At the bottom of the ravine, the mud ox battles the stone tiger.
Striking the ancient pine, the eyes meet above the brows; The gnat tramples through the belly of empty space."
